#99437. 5 High Horsepower Performance Engines That Are Seemingly Indestructible

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1466 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

5 High Horsepower Performance Engines That Are Seemingly Indestructible

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1466 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some engines make a lot of horsepower but are as fleeting as a sunset on a warm summer night.
  • It has been revealed that for this list, we picked engines that can take a ton of abuse worry free.
  • Sources indicate that jesse shouldn't have been surprised by the engine under the hood of the mangled Supra Paul Walker's character procured in the first "The Fast and the Furious." All fourth-generation Supras came with 2JZ engines.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some engines make a lot of horsepower but are as fleeting as a sunset on a warm summer night. The BMW S65 V8 found in the E90-generation M3 that needs rod bearings as preventative maintenance comes to mind, as do Subaru's EJ engines, which are 4-cylinders with a terrible reputation for reliability. But in making some of the best performance engines of all time, some manufacturers have over-built their engines so they are good time for a long time.

It has been revealed that for this list, we picked engines that can take a ton of abuse worry free. Some engines, like Toyota's 2JZ-GTE, aren't the most powerful out of the box. But they are under-stressed from the factory, and tuners have more than doubled the engine's output without affecting reliability. Other engines, like the Viper V10, are powerful, reliable, and have an even higher performance ceiling. With that being said, this is not a comprehensive list of brick-house engines by any means. If we missed a motor with a beefcake block, let us know down in the comments.

Sources indicate that jesse shouldn't have been surprised by the engine under the hood of the mangled Supra Paul Walker's character procured in the first "The Fast and the Furious." All fourth-generation Supras came with 2JZ engines. Nonetheless, his excitement was justified. The 2JZ, particularly the factory twin-turbocharged 2JZ-GTE variant, is well known for making substantial power without sacrificing reliability.

Industry observers note that for the U.S. market, the 2JZ-GTE was only found under the hood of the MKIV Supra Turbo, and a little under 7,000 Supra Turbos were sold Stateside. The twin-turbo straight-6 made 320 horsepower from the factory. But it wasn't long before tuners found that the engine was capable of so much more.

The 2JZ's secret sauce largely comes from how its bottom end is constructed. The 2JZ is a closed-deck engine, meaning that the top of the cylinder walls are supported by metal. This, along with the cast iron construction of the 2JZ's engine block, makes the cylinders really strong and able to hold up to a lot of turbo boost. Also, the 2JZ has a forged steel crankshaft. The difference between cast and forged crankshafts comes down to strength and cost. The more common cast crankshaft is cheaper to make, but they are less likely to survive the stresses of an engine outputting significant horsepower long term. All of this over-engineering means that the 2JZ-GTE can make upward of 700 horsepower without touching the bottom end.

When Nissan revived the GT-R nameplate for the 2009 model year, it was a revelation. The all-wheel-drive coupe put down acceleration, braking, and road-holding numbers that bested supercars like the Porsche 911 Turbo and Lamborghini LP640 for a fraction of the cost. The center piece of its performance was the twin-turbo 3.8-liter V6 designated VR38DETT. The new power plant was rated at 480 horsepower and 430 pound-feet of torque. The 0-to-60 times that the GT-R achieved made the automotive press suspect that Nissan low-balled the twin-turbo V6's output. Indeed, when MotorTrend Channel dyno tested a 2009 GT-R, the outlet found that the factory torque figure was underrated by 40 pound-feet.

Nissan took great care in building the VR38DETT. Each all-aluminum engine was hand assembled by expert craftsmen at Nissan's Yokohama plant in Japan. The VR38 is over square , which means that the engine's construction is more suited for high revs. The GT-R's engine has plasma-coated cylinder bores, which reduce friction and improve cooling. Like the 2JZ-GTE, the VR38 has a robust closed-deck engine block.

Also like the 2JZ, tuners found that the VR38DETT could make a lot more horsepower without a ton of extra work. The engine can safely make around 600 horsepower with the factory turbochargers. Anything above that and you'll be swapping turbos and replacing the connecting rods, which are a known weak point above 650 foot-pounds of torque. The good news is that once the rods are taken care of, the factory block can withstand more than 1,000 hp.

According to recent reports, when Porsche debuted its race-car-for-the-road GT3 in 1999, it equipped its most hardcore 911 with a race-proven engine. The GT3 ditched the standard 911's then-new water-cooled flat-6 engine for a power plant based on the Le Mans-winning 911 GT1, which, in turn, was derived from the engine found in the dominant 962 Group C racer. The engine initially displaced 3.6-liters and output 360 horsepower.

Since it shares the same M96 designation as the engine in the back of the standard 911, enthusiasts call the race-derived engine "Mezger," after Porsche's engine guru Hans Mezger. He was behind the design of the 962 engine, as well as the power plants in the original 911, the 917 race car, and McLaren's 1983-to-1987 F1 entries. In 2000, Porsche strapped a pair of turbochargers to the Mezger for the 911 Turbo, which was good for 415 hp. Porsche used the Mezger in the GT2, GT3, and Turbo until 2013. The ultimate factory Mezger was the turbocharged GT2 RS that made 612 hp. If that's not enough, tuners regularly extract 1,000-plus horsepower out of the Mezger.

Over the years, the engine has gained a reputation for its reliability. The reasons why the Mezger flat-6 is bulletproof come down to its construction. First off, the Mezger has a gear-driven intermediate shaft (IMS) with a plain bearing that is always lubricated by engine oil. The unit won't fail catastrophically like the problematic, sealed IMS bearings that plague the M96 and M97 engines found in lesser, contemporary 911s. The Mezger also has a more rigid, reinforced crankcase compared to the standard sixes. And it has individual, pressed-in cylinder liners that are easier to replace than the bores in the standard engine.

What can be stated that hasn't already been said about Chevrolet's venerable LS V8? It's powerful, compact, and has an abundant aftermarket. The inciting incident for the LS was the 375-horsepower Lotus-designed LT5 V8 in the ZR-1. The good ol' boys on Chevy's internal small-block V8 team were miffed , so they decided to do something that wouldn't have Chevy going to an outside contractor for the 'Vette ever again. The team designed an all-aluminum pushrod V8 , dubbed the LS1, from the ground up. When the LS1 was introduced in the 1997 Corvette, it was only down 30 horsepower compared to the more exotic, quad-cam LT5.

GM adapted the LS architecture for numerous applications over its 18-year run. As such, LS-architecture V8s were available in a bunch of different flavors, from iron-block 4.8-liter truck motors to all-aluminum 7.0-liter Corvette mills. The most powerful factory variant, the LS9, made 638 hp with help from a 2.3-liter Roots-type supercharger. But crate engines from Chevrolet Performance like the LSX-454R can make over 700 hp without boost.

According to recent reports, the LS in any iteration is a strong base for a performance build. 15 years ago, Hot Rod famously turbocharged a stock-bottom-end 4.8-liter to 1,200 horsepower. Part of the reason for the resilience of that poor 4.8 is that LS engines have six-bolt main bearing caps. The main caps help secure the crankshaft in the block, so, generally speaking, the more bolts that hold the caps, the stronger the bottom end. And it's not just the bottom end. The LS has a valve train that is capable of revving to 7,000 rpm from the factory.

When the Dodge Viper came out in 1992, there was nothing quite like it. It was a 400-horsepower missile that was the the closest thing to a modern Shelby Cobra. The secret to the Viper's prodigious power? An all-aluminum 8.0-liter V10. Lamborghini, a subsidiary of Chrysler at the time, helped  design the V10's aluminum block. Displacement and power figures of the V10 grew throughout the years, with the final Viper ACRs displacing a staggering 8.4 liters and outputting 645 horsepower.

According to recent reports, as exotic as an all-aluminum V10 sounds, the Viper engine is known for its reliability, unlike some of the fussy mills in its Italian supercar counterparts. That's not surprising, given the Viper V10 is based on Mopar's LA series V8s. Like the LA engines, the Viper's power plant has two valves per cylinder that are actuated by pushrods. In other words, the engine's architecture is about as simple as it gets.

In a recent development, at more-than-factory horsepower, some Viper V10s are better than others. The V10s built prior to 2000 have forged pistons, which are better able to withstand the stresses from forced induction. Forged pistons didn't reappear until the last generation Viper (2013 to 2017) was blessed with them again. Regardless of which engine you have, suppliers like D.S.S. Racing will be happy to sell you forged pistons that will hold up to boost.

Three Green Hydrogen Projects Slip Through The Trump Chopper

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1475 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that when US President Donald Trump swept into office last year, he set his choppers upon the $8 billion Regional Clean Hydrogen Hubs program, snuffing out prepares to establish a diversified, domestic hydrogen market with a focus on decarbonization.
  • If you guessed the startup Plug Power is in the mix, run right out and buy yourself a cigar.
  • It has been revealed that plug Power soon pivoted into replacing gas-derived hydrogen fuel with so-named green hydrogen, pushed from water by an electrical current.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when US President Donald Trump swept into office last year, he set his choppers upon the $8 billion Regional Clean Hydrogen Hubs program, snuffing out prepares to establish a diversified, domestic hydrogen market with a focus on decarbonization. Nevertheless, some stakeholders have continued to pursue the dream of producing green hydrogen from renewable resources — instead of squeezing it from natural gas. Now all that hard work is beginning to pay off, Trump or no Trump.

If you guessed the startup Plug Power is in the mix, run right out and buy yourself a cigar. Plug Power began life back in 1997 with a focus on electric forklifts powered by zero emission hydrogen fuel cells. In addition to replacing fossil fuels, Plug Power aimed to replace battery-powered forklifts, with fuel cells being a better fit for the fast-paced environment of shipping and logistics.

It has been revealed that plug Power soon pivoted into replacing gas-derived hydrogen fuel with so-named green hydrogen, pushed from water by an electrical current. After a series of ups and downs the tech giant hit the jackpot in January of 2025, when the US Department of Energy tapped it for a $1.66 loan guarantee in support of the Regional Clean Hydrogen Hubs program, which was funded through the 2021 Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. If all went according to plan, Plug Power would have used the loan to finance up to six green hydrogen projects around the US, all affiliated with the Hydrogen Hubs program.

So much for that. The Energy Department unveiled the loan award at the beginning of the month, when former President Joe Biden was still in office. However, by the end of the month Trump was officially installed in the White House. He soon pulled the plug on the Plug Power loan, so to speak, sending it down the drain alongside many other federally funded clean power projects.

It has been revealed that that was not the end of the story for Plug Power. After all, it’s a big world out there, and Plug Power continued to pitch its wares overseas. Last week the manufacturer also relaunched itself back into the US market, bigly.

According to recent reports, on November 17, Plug Power declared that its fresh “GenEco™ Scale” green hydrogen electrolyzer system is up for grabs in the US market while concurrently announcing that its first customer is the Texas-based firm Aracdia eFuels. Arcadia will deploy 280 megawatts’ worth of GenEco Scale modules at its Project ARC campus in the Portland/Corpus Christi area in Texas. When fully up and running, Project ARC will deploy green hydrogen from the GenEco Scale system to produce about 23.2 million gallons of fossil-free aviation fuel per year.

While green hydrogen has its fans in the decarbonization field, the stubbornly high cost of electrolysis has raised a formidable obstacle against widespread commercial uptake. Plug Power is among the stakeholders pitching modular, integrated systems to help bring costs down into parity with conventional hydrogen sourced from natural gas or coal, and that’s where the GenEco system comes into play.

“Built around a standardized 20 MW block architecture, GenEco Scale combines Plug’s proven proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolyzer technology with integrated balance-of-plant systems into a modular, pre-engineered solution for hydrogen production projects of approximately 100 MW and above,” Plug Power explained in a press statement last week. The manufacturer also noted that the “outdoor-ready” system avoids much of the cost and time related to the buildings and other infrastructure required of traditional large scale electrolyzer systems.

Arcadia eFuels CEO Amy Hebert also chipped in her two cents in support of the modular system. “Reducing the engineering burden on our EPC [engineering, procurement, and construction] partners and minimizing the complexity of bringing these systems together were important considerations for Project ARC,” Herbert emphasized.

Savings on land is another part of the cost-cutting strategy. Unlike conventional electrolyzer system layouts, the GenEco model deploys a vertical configuration. The vertical system requires less than one acre per 100 megawatts of electrolyzer capacity, according to Plug Power.

Another Plug Power project has bubbled up in California, which was on track to host a suite of projects under the Hydrogen Hubs program with a focus on hydrogen derived from biomass as well as water electrolysis. The funding evaporated under Trump, but the state is still getting its hands on green hydrogen.

On November 19, Plug Power declared that its containerized 5-megawatt GenEco electrolyzer is up and running at a green hydrogen plant in Vernon, California, under the umbrella of the Newly introduced Jersey-based firm Avina Clean Hydrogen.

It has been revealed that green hydrogen from this project will go to fulfill California’s plans for a zero-emission freight corridor, the proposal for which includes fuel cell electric trucks as well as battery-powered trucks. “Located approximately 10 miles from the Port of Long Beach, the facility is designed to serve fleets moving freight through the Los Angeles–Long Beach port complex. It combines on-site fueling with tube-trailer deliveries to customers across the Los Angeles region,” Plug Power explains.

The station, also accommodate buses, and it can refuel a heavy-duty vehicle to more than 95% capacity in less than 30 minutes, according to Plug Power. That stacks up well against charging times for battery-powered heavy duty vehicles. On its website, for example, Tesla asserts that its newly introduced Semi electric truck can recover 60% of its 500 mile range in up to 30 minutes at a Tesla Megacharger station.

In a recent development, for the record, Avina has not placed all of its cards on hydrogen fuel cell trucks. The tech giant’s roster of clean hydrogen projects also includes SAF (sustainable aviation fuel) and green ammonia, which is a key input for fertilizer among other chemical products.

According to recent reports, rounding out the trio of new projects is the Swedish firm PowerCell Group. The firm is better known for its work in the marine energy field, and now it is tapping into land-based markets as well. Last week PowerCell confirmed that its US branch is in motion to set up a green hydrogen system run by excess electricity from an existing solar array owned by a to-be-named client in the US. In effect, the hydrogen will serve as an energy storage medium. It will go to run a PowerCell PowerPod 3000 stationary fuel cell, which will kick into action at night to keep the clean kilowatts flowing after the sun goes down.

PowerCell describes the PowerPod 3000 as “a containerized power generation platform integrating our PS190 systems with power conversion equipment, cooling and DMC, PowerCell’s control and Energy Orchestration technology,” with an installed fuel cell capacity of 27 megawatts and 20 megawatts of rated power.

Sources indicate that that’s a good question. Rather than let that excess solar electricity go to waste, the client could invest in a BESS (battery energy storage system) for daytime energy storage and night-time electricity. However, a typical BESS only lasts for a handful of hours. In contrast, PowerCell describes its fuel cell as a “long duration” storage system, which generally means eight hours or more.

PowerCell also points out that a fuel cell does something that a BESS cannot. Fuel cells generate electricity by combining hydrogen with oxygen in the presence of a catalyst. Water — H2O — is a byproduct. All else being equal, that opens up the potential for green hydrogen to serve as a water distribution medium, sucking up water in an electrolysis system at one location, then pushing it out in a fuel cell located elsewhere.

PowerCell is not making any specific promises for this particular project, though the organization does emphasize that “the ability to generate both electricity and recoverable water adds another dimension of value to hydrogen-based energy storage.”.

“The amount of water recovered, and its potential uses will depend on the final system configuration, operating conditions and water treatment requirements,” the tech giant adds.

And, that’s where things get interesting. The client is a to-be-named electric cooperative, which is of interest because electric cooperatives (more specifically, Rural Electric Cooperatives) account for a large portion of the US grid, and their roots in the rural poverty fighting programs of the Great Depression provide for a distinctive public benefit mission that can, in some cases, allow more wiggle room for innovative energy solutions that generate broad benefits for local communities.

I’m reaching out to PowerCell for more details. If they can’t divulge the name of the client yet, perhaps they’ll be able to describe what they mean by long duration energy storage, so stay tuned for an enhancement.

Marc Marquez Crowns Himself GOAT After Equalling MotoGP Title Record

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that no championship fight is ever over until it's over.
  • It has been revealed that if it weren't for his history-making triumph, it would have been a weekend at Portimão to forget for Marquez.
  • Aprilia's Marco Bezzecchi swept the weekend in Portugal, winning the sprint and feature races from pole.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that no championship fight is ever over until it's over. Marc Marquez clinched the 2026 MotoGP World Championship on Sunday after finishing eighth at the Portuguese Grand Prix. The Spaniard overcame a record 106-point deficit to win his eighth MotoGP title and his tenth world championship across all Grand Prix classes. Marquez's eighth top-class crown ties in the record books with Giacomo Agostini, the sport's greatest of all time. In true MotoGP fashion, the post-race championship fits the moment's monumental nature.

It has been revealed that if it weren't for his history-making triumph, it would have been a weekend at Portimão to forget for Marquez. He had the opportunity to win the championship during Saturday's sprint race, but dramatically pushed the title fight to Sunday. In damp conditions, Marquez was riding in third with only a lap and a half to go when his factory Ducati slid out from under him at Turn 7. He and his bike went off into the gravel. Thankfully for his title hopes, the Spaniard was fine. Seeing how his coronation could be canceled, Marquez took no chances during the feature. He bolted to the lead at the start, then cruised home.

Aprilia's Marco Bezzecchi swept the weekend in Portugal, winning the sprint and feature races from pole. However, eighth place was enough for Marquez to win the title. According to Motorsport.com, he said post-race. "Yesterday was a massive warning, so today I said 'f*** off' [to] the race. I didn't care about the result. I just I wanted to close the championship.".

Relief and ecstasy overcame Marquez after he crossed the finish line and was mobbed by his fellow competitors, trackside marshals and Ducati personnel. As is MotoGP tradition, there was an elaborate celebration for the champion. He climbed atop a platform to don a gold-trimmed jersey in front of his adoring fans, picking up a microphone to thank them. Marquez then trotted over to a massive videoboard to watch a crash-filled career highlight reel, which featured Valentino Rossi's infamous 2015 kick.

The celebration's finale saw Marquez climb a ten-step staircase, recognizing his ten world championships, with the shadow of a goat behind him. At the summit, Agostini emerged from a hidden door to present Marquez with a golden helmet. He then rode his Ducati to the championship stage with a Spanish flag in hand, screaming his lungs out.

It has been revealed that sunday was arguably the capstone moment of Marquez's career. While the 33-year-old signed a two-year extension to remain at Ducati through the 2028 season, no one can guarantee that he will win another world championship. He was nearly cut short after breaking his arm in 2020. The allure of a tenth world title has proven to be a specter that haunts MotoGP's recent greats. His long-time rival Valentino Rossi spent a dozen years trying to win his tenth world title. Despite retiring in 2021, the legendary Italian still can't let go of his 2015 title fight and feud with Marquez.

Pondering The Potential Of Plug-In VPP

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1398 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I recently discussed the potential of the plug-in VPP from Jackery and Every Electric to transform urban energy storage.
  • It has been revealed that essentially, customers of the plug-in VPP receive a battery, plug it into the wall and their window air conditioner, and connect to Wi-Fi.
  • It has been revealed that both Jackery and Every Electric are collaborating and working to create innovative solutions for customer needs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I recently discussed the potential of the plug-in VPP from Jackery and Every Electric to transform urban energy storage. But the current program could be just the start. The more I discussed it at RE+, the more it started making me thing about where it could go in the future.

It has been revealed that essentially, customers of the plug-in VPP receive a battery, plug it into the wall and their window air conditioner, and connect to Wi-Fi. Then they use AC as they normally would, the VPP shaves off demand peaks on the grid, and the customer gets paid. It is likely the fastest, easiest and cheapest way to implement urban BESS in the US. And regular people living in apartments benefit. You can read more about the plug-in VPP in my previous article for context. Or you can watch the video below.

It has been revealed that both Jackery and Every Electric are collaborating and working to create innovative solutions for customer needs. Plug-in VPP makes the benefits of battery storage accessible to people in apartments. However, the potential could go much farther. Of note, much of what I am discussing here is not available yet. But the plug-in VPP sparked my imagination, and I wanted to expand on what might be possible.

Initially, the system is being deployed in New York City, which has a large number of apartments that can be aggregated to create a meaningful amount of combined storage. Of course, the potential can be realized in areas outside of NYC. Every Electric is already looking to expand into the Boston area. There are several other areas where the existing system based on window air conditioners in urban areas could apply, particularly along the Northeast corridor. However, as the program evolves, there is tremendous potential outside of the region.

It has been revealed that in Jackery’s home state of California, 4.5 TWh of solar and wind power was curtailed in the first half of 2026. More electricity wasted in six months in one state than many developing countries consume in an entire year. Residential solar often feeds into the grid when it just leads to curtailments elsewhere. Even with recent ESS installations, the Duck Curve is still deepening. If home batteries can help “decapitate the duck,” customers and the utility both stand to benefit. And all that renewable energy currently being wasted can contribute to reducing emissions.

According to recent reports, in addition, every Jackery battery can operate as a solar generator, with a DC input. People can simply plug in a solar panel or two to recharge the battery. No additional inverter needed. As it does not send energy back into the grid, it also avoids the cost and complication of traditional grid-tied systems. Sending solar power directly to the battery would avoid having excess solar generation fed into the grid that contributes to overcapacity, deepening the back of the duck curve. Demand response could then come from a battery charged largely from solar, rather than from the grid. As the US is still trying to figure out balcony solar regulations, this would let people enjoy many of the benefits of small scale, plug-and-play solar now. No electricians needed.

Of course, when balcony solar regulations are figured out, Jackery has solutions like the SolarVault3 that I saw at IFA Berlin. Potentially, this system could integrate with point of use battery storage to form a kind of hybrid plug-in system. In the process, solar power could be utilized when it does the most for the grid and offers the greatest potential payback for the customer.

Recent findings suggest that there is also a lot of potential for this concept to work outside of the US. In many parts of the world, most people live in apartments. As the planet warms, world cooling needs recently overtook heating for the first time. As the VPP is monitored via a Wi-Fi connection, there is no need to upgrade to a smart meter to take advantage of the capability. As the storage is already distributed, there is also reduced need to provide the grid upgrades to distribute the energy stored in a large battery during peak energy demand.

Recent findings suggest that at the moment, the plug-in VPP is only working with one model of battery in one application. That makes the deployment and scaling of the plug-in VPP easier. Large urban areas offer the clearest path to aggregate the storage needed for a plug-in VPP to work.

Sources indicate that however, Jackery has sold over 8 million units over the past 15 years. This has established a level of customer trust and a reputation for reliability. Many of those portable power stations and solar generators can connect to Wi-Fi. That is potentially GWh of deployable storage.

Industry observers note that in addition, portable power stations are very popular now. Many Jackery models are selling out. Preparedness is a major driver. Climate-related disasters amplify the fear and uncertainty. However, the batteries that people are buying to be prepared for emergencies offer far greater potential capability. The more batteries that are out there, the greater the potential.

According to recent reports, as the software and capability of the VPP develop, multiple batteries have the potential to connect to amplify value, even if that capability isn’t being offered yet. Those batteries, in coordination with a VPP, could earn people money. Currently, the system is being run with one battery model, but Jackery offers a wide range of batteries with Wi-Fi connectivity that might be able to participate in the future. Once the program has proven itself with the initial application in urban areas, there is potential for expansion.

Sources indicate that as people start earning money, even if they purchased the battery out of preparedness concerns, they would also start to see the broader benefit. When they gain both confidence and financial benefit from battery storage and renewable energy, they will tend to rationalize that benefit. That can lead to a broader shift in mindset. When you try to start with a rational argument, especially when that argument involves added costs, people are less likely to be supportive than if you start with the benefit.

Many of the pieces to make this happen have already existed. People have the ability to program Jackery batteries through the app to charge and discharge during certain parts of the day. This can work with TOU utility plans, where available. But it doesn’t take full advantage of the capabilities of a VPP. Customers do not get full credit for the storage capability. The true innovation comes from putting the pieces together, between the Jackery hardware, Every Electric software and the utility. If one of those pieces of the collaboration was missing, a plug-in VPP wouldn’t have the same potential.

One of the things that has impressed me about Jackery since I was first introduced to the company was their focus on solving customer problems. However, to create solutions, they also recognize that collaboration is often necessary. I already saw this with the flexible solar panels of SunBooster at IFA Berlin for balcony solar applications, and then again with Every Electric for plug-in VPP.

I asked Jackery founder and CEO Jack Sun about the value of collaboration in creating an environmentally friendly ecosystem:.

This is also very key, because we have an open model, and we are more willing and more innovative….

We will actively collaborate with partners in areas such as power chips and more proactively in co-creation. We aim to accelerate the application of their innovations into our solar generator solutions. Our goal is to achieve faster and more efficient solar energy development through joint innovation. The generator can be installed in every household to help more families achieve energy independence more cost-effectively, while also reducing carbon emissions more swiftly.

Industry observers note that this focus on collaboration makes meaningful innovation happen. Just as I speculated here on the potential of plug-in VPP, other people will have their own ideas. Some will be different than this VPP concept. Many will be better ideas than the ideas I can come up with. Having innovative companies like Jackery and Every Electric actively seeking to work with partners creates potential for those ideas to come together. I look forward to seeing what new solutions come together next.

Fresh Homes Are Now $40K Cheaper Than Existing Homes

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Newly introduced-construction homes are less expensive than existing ones, and the difference has never been larger, the National Association of Home Builders has found.
  • According to recent reports, last month's NAHB/Wells Fargo Cost of Housing Index found the median newly introduced-home price is $393,300, compared to a median-priced existing home, which comes to $432,900 in the third quarter of 2026.
  • Builders, struggling to find buyers, are digging deeper to offer incentives on new homes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Newly introduced-construction homes are less expensive than existing ones, and the difference has never been larger, the National Association of Home Builders has found.

According to recent reports, last month's NAHB/Wells Fargo Cost of Housing Index found the median newly introduced-home price is $393,300, compared to a median-priced existing home, which comes to $432,900 in the third quarter of 2026. That's the largest difference between new- and existing-home prices in the history of NAHB's tracking, Chairman Bill Owens stated.

Builders, struggling to find buyers, are digging deeper to offer incentives on new homes. The National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index plunged to a 14-year low last week. Many of the nation's major homebuilders have reported large year-over-year declines in revenue. But housing starts continue apace, showing some hope for the market long term.

“Builders are working with buyers to make latest homes more affordable and appealing in a tough market, yet the latest CHI data show housing costs still overburden families,” NAHB Chief Economist Robert Dietz stated in a statement.

According to recent reports, A typical family would have to pay 36% of their income for a median-priced existing home. They'd need 33% of their income for a fresh home, a drop of 1% from the second quarter. And that accounts for a $17,000 drop in the median new-home price in the second quarter, when it was $434,900, NAHB found.

“As builders contend with rising construction costs, tighter lending standards and persistent labor shortages, policymakers should remove regulatory obstacles, enact permitting reform and create a stronger business environment that enables builders to produce more attainable, affordable homes,” Dietz said.

Housing costs across the board are rising. Owners are also struggling to manage insurance costs, HOA fees, and utilities.

NAHB's data shows that the San Jose, CA, area is the most cost-burdened market in the third quarter, and 79% of a typical family's income is needed to make a mortgage payment on an existing home. Honolulu, San Diego, San Fransisco, and Barnstable Town, MA, follow. All are above 60%.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, the least cost-burdened market is Decatur, IL, where 17% of a typical family's income is needed to make a mortgage payment on an existing home. Elmira, NY, Peoria, IL, Wichita Falls, TX, and Springfield, IL, all also sit under 20%.

According to recent reports, NAHB studied 175 markets and found that, in 95 of them, the typical family is cost-burdened, meaning they spend more than 31% of their income on a median-priced existing home. Eight of those markets are severely cost-burdened, where they pay more than 50%.

Owens said that price cuts and incentives are improving affordability. But the nation needs more pro-building laws to solve the underlying problem.

It has been revealed that "According to our latest survey, 43% cut prices in October—the highest share since 2020—and 65% offered sales incentives," Owens said. "But policymakers must do more to reduce red tape, address labor shortages, and fix supply chains so builders can expand the nation’s housing supply.”.

Part of the story is that it's a rough housing market all around.

Recent findings suggest that the average rate on 30-year fixed home loans jumped to 7.28% last week, up from 7.11% recorded the week before and 6.26% last year, according to Freddie Mac. Pending home sales fell to a record low in October, and existing-home sales hit their lowest level since 2010.

Sources indicate that but part of the story is also how builders have changed up their business. The latest Realtor.com® quarterly construction insights report finds that existing homes are more expensive than fresh ones based on the price per square foot: $218 for new homes, $219 for existing ones.

Realtor.com senior economist Joel Berner writes that this month's upcoming-construction data points to builders expecting tough conditions to continue.

According to recent reports, "Builders are dealing with a litany of obstacles to selling homes, whether it’s rising costs of land, labor, and materials, high financing costs, or weak buyer demand," Berner notes. "This month’s data shows them slowing down activity at the top of their funnel, which will result in slower months of starts and completions later on.".

Industry observers note that tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

What Happens To The Cars A Dealership Can't Sell?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (757 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Americans buy about 16 million fresh cars every year, barring the occasional economic upheaval or global pandemic.
  • It varies by company, but many dealers consider 60 to 90 days on the lot long enough for a car to count as aged inventory.
  • It has been revealed that there wasn't always a reason for what made a slow seller.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Americans buy about 16 million fresh cars every year, barring the occasional economic upheaval or global pandemic. Yet, that heady number doesn't take into account that not every car sells like manufacturers and dealers hope. Some models languish on lots for months or even years. One of the first things dealers try is offering customers a discount. At the dealership where I sold new and used cars, the bosses would also offer incentives to salespeople to move cars that just couldn't gain traction. More aggressive tactics like converting the car into a service loaner or demonstrator could also come into play. Then, surrender might come in the form of trading the car to another dealer or sending the vehicle to a wholesale auction. In case you're wondering, bidding at these dealer-only auctions usually requires a license.

Used cars can sit around, too. What's considered a slow seller? It varies by company, but many dealers consider 60 to 90 days on the lot long enough for a car to count as aged inventory. At my dealership, management started to get anxious at the 60-day mark. Why? Because most dealers don't own their inventories outright. The cars you see on the lot and in storage yards are financed. It's called floorplanning, which contributes a significant amount to the overhead. Last year, the average floorplan costs for a upcoming car were about $237 per month. That amount swiftly eats into profits as the months accumulate.

It has been revealed that there wasn't always a reason for what made a slow seller. Sometimes, it was the color (the used car manager was prohibited from buying anything brown) or the lack of a particular option. Pricing was always a factor. An overpriced, unpopular model is a direct cause of crickets chirping.

Money has a way of motivating customers and salespeople when it comes to old inventory. Sometimes, extra discounts or a better trade-in valuation is all it takes. In my selling days, management would also tack on bonuses on aged units. If someone came in hell-bent on the best deal possible and was less focused on the car (yes, those buyers exist), I would steer them toward these options. It was usually a win for everyone.

According to recent reports, yet, money can't fix everything. In these situations, the choice could involve taking the problematic latest car out of inventory and doing something else with it. The typical routes are making the car a service loaner or letting a manager drive it as a demonstrator. After a time, the vehicle may then make its way back to the lot, but sometimes on the used car side of the business. Demonstrator units typically go up for sale before the odometer hits 3,000 miles. It may be sold as new if it was never registered, but the high-for-a-new-car mileage usually comes with a disclosure and a discount.

In a recent development, at the dealership I worked at, the tech giant also had a thriving car rental division (they were stingy with loaner cars), so it wasn't unusual to see older units positioned there. In theory, any of these steps could be taken with slow-selling used cars, but from my experience, dealers often use newer models for loaners, demonstrators, or rentals.

Sources indicate that if discounts and incentives can't move older upcoming inventory and changing over to loaners isn't practical, dealers use other measures to get the offending car off the lot. Dealers trade vehicles with each other. It's a common practice among franchised dealers. A slow-seller in one market might be the right model for another. The transaction could be a vehicle swap with a cash payment for any difference in value, or the other dealer will just make an outright purchase. My dealership had relationships with several other same-brand retailers outside our immediate trading area.

In a recent development, wholesale auctions are the last-resort inventory disposal method. At this point, the dealership has decided to cut its losses. However, the bleeding can get worse. There are costs to bring a car to auction (fees and transportation costs). Also, an auction may not fetch a satisfactory price. It can be a gamble.

Industry observers note that specialized auctions for franchised dealers from the same brand also exist. Upcoming cars can go to auction, too. Minnesota statute, for example, allows dealers in that state to auction new vehicles. For used cars, outlets like Manheim and Openlane let dealers offload unsuccessful inventory. ADESA, which Carvana bought a few years ago, is another.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the wind energy industry matures, operators and service providers are increasingly focused on maximizing turbine availability while controlling long-term maintenance costs.
  • Heat exchangers play a critical role in maintaining proper oil temperature and viscosity within wind turbine gearboxes.
  • It has been revealed that “Wind operators today are balancing increasing performance expectations with the realities of aging fleets and rising maintenance costs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the wind energy industry matures, operators and service providers are increasingly focused on maximizing turbine availability while controlling long-term maintenance costs. Although major drivetrain components often receive the spotlight, one overlooked system can have an outsized impact on turbine reliability and performance: gearbox oil cooling.

Heat exchangers play a critical role in maintaining proper oil temperature and viscosity within wind turbine gearboxes. When cooling systems become clogged with airborne debris, dust, or organic material, oil temperatures rise, lubrication performance declines, and component stress increases. Over time, these conditions can contribute to reduced gearbox efficiency, elevated maintenance demands, and avoidable downtime.

It has been revealed that “Wind operators today are balancing increasing performance expectations with the realities of aging fleets and rising maintenance costs. Technologies that improve cooling efficiency and reduce service exposure can have a meaningful impact on long-term turbine reliability and operational profitability,” according to Mike Erickson, HYDAC’s Market Manager for the Wind Industry.

Recent findings suggest that traditional “panel cut” heat exchanger designs have long been susceptible to clogging due to their tightly packed fin structures. In many wind environments — particularly agricultural, dusty, or high-pollen regions — debris accumulation can severely restrict airflow. Oil leaks can further compound the problem by trapping contaminants within the exchanger core, making cleaning more difficult and labor intensive.

This operational challenge has driven the need for more resilient cooling technologies designed specifically for real-world wind farm conditions.

In a recent development, HYDAC’s new “Square Wave” heat exchanger design represents a significant advancement in addressing these reliability concerns. Engineered to allow debris to pass more freely through the exchanger fins, the design minimizes clogging while improving cooling efficiency under demanding operating conditions.

The importance of effective cooling cannot be overstated. Wind turbine gearbox oil typically operates within an optimal temperature range of approximately 45°C to 65°C. Even modest temperature increases can significantly impact oil viscosity. According to field data, a 12°C rise in oil temperature can reduce viscosity by nearly 28 percent — affecting lubrication quality and accelerating wear on critical drivetrain components.

In a recent development, field trials have demonstrated measurable operational benefits from the Square Wave design. During a one-year trial on GE 1.x turbines, the upgraded exchanger consistently reduced clogging and lowered maintenance requirements compared to traditional panel cut cores. Operators reported reduced up-tower cleaning time and fewer temperature-related cooling faults.

In a recent development, field validation across multiple turbine platforms has further reinforced the operational advantages of the Square Wave design. In one case study involving legacy 1 MW-class turbines operating in the Pacific Northwest, a major renewable energy operator installed pilot sets of Square Wave heat exchangers as part of a cooling performance evaluation. Installation teams reported the upgraded exchangers integrated seamlessly into the existing platform with no retrofit complications.

Industry observers note that after initial operating data demonstrated improved cooling consistency, the operator expanded the evaluation program with additional units. Long-term SCADA analysis later showed turbines equipped with Square Wave technology operate approximately 20 to 25 percent cooler than comparable turbines using conventional heat exchanger designs under similar operating conditions. The data also highlighted another notable advantage: the Square Wave cores continued to maintain airflow and cooling efficiency in debris-heavy environments where traditional exchanger designs became increasingly restricted over time.

The successful deployment also generated interest from additional wind service organizations seeking retrofit-ready cooling upgrades that could improve turbine reliability while reducing maintenance burdens across aging fleets.

“What operators are increasingly recognizing is that small improvements in thermal management can create meaningful gains in turbine reliability, maintenance efficiency, and long-term asset performance,” said Erickson. “The field data we’re seeing continues to validate the value of designing cooling systems specifically for real-world wind operating environments.”.

It has been revealed that more recently, long-term SCADA data from Mitsubishi platforms further validated the technology’s performance. After two years of operation, turbines equipped with Square Wave heat exchangers operated approximately 19 to 25 percent cooler than reference turbines using standard exchanger designs under comparable operating conditions.

For wind asset owners and service providers, the implications are substantial: Improved thermal management supports healthier oil viscosity, more stable gearbox operation, and potentially longer component life. At the same time, reduced cleaning frequency and fewer cooling-related service events translate directly into lower operational expenditures and increased turbine availability.

Recent findings suggest that as the industry continues to prioritize lifecycle optimization and energy production efficiency, innovative subsystem upgrades such as advanced heat exchanger technology are becoming increasingly valuable. Rather than waiting for costly failures or performance degradation, operators are seeking practical retrofit solutions that improve reliability without requiring major system redesigns.

“Effective thermal management is critical to protecting gearbox health and maintaining oil performance over time. By addressing one of the most common causes of cooling degradation — debris accumulation — operators can improve uptime while reducing unnecessary maintenance interventions,” noted HYDAC’s Erickson.

According to recent reports, for wind stakeholders evaluating ways to improve gearbox reliability, reduce maintenance exposure, and enhance turbine performance, cooling system optimization deserves greater attention. Proven retrofit technologies like advanced heat exchanger designs can offer a practical path toward improved uptime and operational efficiency without requiring major system overhauls.

Industry observers note that as fleets age and performance expectations continue to rise, collaboration between operators, service providers, and technology partners will be essential to building more resilient wind assets for the future. Army says it looks to detonate degraded lead in Iowa town no later than Nov. 24, despite court stay.

Sources indicate that des Moines, IOWA — The Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club, and Earthjustice will continue to advocate for accountability from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the U.S. Army in the planned detonation of lead azide in Middletown, Iowa. Early Sunday morning, the groups filed declarations with the court that call out the Army’s inadequate public notice and information, and question the Army’s and EPA’s claims that all alternatives were given appropriate consideration.

It has been revealed that the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) filed a statement with the court late on Saturday, Nov. 21, indicating that the Army intends to invoke emergency provisions of the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) to detonate 9,773.5 pounds of lead azide stored at the Iowa Army Ammunitions Plant, without a permit from the EPA. According to the DOJ’s court filings, the Army intends to do so no later than Nov. 24. On Nov. 20, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals granted Earthjustice’s request to put on hold a permit allowing the Army to detonate.

It has been revealed that “People across numerous impacted communities speaking up and demanding accountability is the only reason there was an opportunity to pause and think about better ways to approach the lead azide problem,” said Earthjustice Attorney Thien Chau. “Yet despite claiming public safety is its top priority and public communication is essential to trust, the Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public’s demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm.”.

This emergency is of the Army’s own making. The Army has not publicly provided details about why the lead azide was not disposed of before it became so dangerous. The Army’s own storage and inspection practices allowed a primary explosive to sit until it reportedly degraded to the point that any alternative disposal method is now deemed too dangerous. The lack of transparency raises real questions about the scope and extent of potential impacts.

“The new information from the DOJ indicates that the problem is significantly worse than the Army originally shared. It appears that detonation may be, at this point, the only feasible option due to how long this problem was allowed to persist. The public deserves to know immediately which communities will be impacted and how residents can most effectively protect themselves and mitigate impacts on their health and homes,” said Michael Schmidt, General Counsel for the Iowa Environmental Council.

The Army knew about this stockpile of dangerous munitions waste for years, and it knew since at least March that the material was becoming unstable. Yet, just one week ago, most Iowans — including those directly in the path of a toxic lead plume, the Iowa governor, and key state agencies and officials — were unaware the Army intended to detonate nearly five tons of lead azide.

The environmental groups argue the EPA and Army permitting documents have not demonstrated, nor provided appropriate documentation that all other safer alternatives to mitigate the material were thoroughly explored.

“The Army has clearly mishandled this situation, and Iowans and residents in our neighboring states deserve a full review of all of the missteps that led us to this point. However, if detonation is now the only option, it is imperative that everyone impacted has access to the full range of testing, mitigation, and remediation resources,” stated Wally Taylor, Attorney and Legal Chair for the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter.

Industry observers note that as of 11 a.m. CST on Sunday, Nov. 22, the Army has failed to provide the public with updated weather modeling and mapping showing the path of the lead dust plume, which means people impacted have little time to take precautions to protect their families and homes. The wind patterns have shifted significantly, which means that potential community exposures have likely changed without visible effort by the Army to provide updated information to the public.

Sources indicate that during the tragic downfall and eventual demise of Saab, Sweden's other quirky and safety conscious car company, the automaker passed through different owners including Dutch supercar maker Spyker and a Chinese real estate giant, neither of which were able to save the brand. As Saab's remnants, under the name of National Electric Vehicle Sweden (NEVS), were circling the proverbial drain, engineers were able to muster one final design: an electric luxury sedan called the Emily GT. The design looked poised to go into production a few years ago thanks to a Canadian startup company called EV Electra, but that also eventually ran out of funding, too.

Sources indicate that now, following some of the final 9-3s and other more boring models being sold, the entire NEVS Emily GT project is being auctioned to the highest bidder, including prototype vehicles, spare parts, tools, and engineering drawings. First reported by the UK-based publication Car, the Swedish auction tech giant Klaravik will open the Emily GT project auction on November 25, and the ad says international companies are welcome to place bids on the project, so any one of you could be the one to save the final Saab that never happened.

We've rooted for the Emily GT since these prototypes were first revealed to the world back in 2023 as a big, powerful, sleek sedan with individual electric motors driving each individual wheel. NEVS planned to power these four motors with a hulking 175-kWh battery pack and aimed for a maximum range of over 500 miles, and it was all wrapped up in vaguely Saab-esque styling with blacked-out A-pillars and upswept headlights that look faintly reminiscent of the final-generation Saab 9-5's headlights.

The auction includes the only four complete NEVS Emily GT prototype vehicles in existence, a sick-looking camouflaged Saab 9-3 powertrain mule, and "a large number of bodies, parts, tools, accessories, and drawings." It's unlikely that this auction will actually result in the revival of our dear, sweet Saab automobiles, but a guy can dream.

Industry observers note that A separate, much less interesting NEVS project will also be joining the Emily GT on the auction block: the Pons autonomous mobility vehicle. The separate Pons auction includes the only Sango prototype ever produced which looks like a more curvaceous Zoox Robotaxi, if that's more your sort of thing.

Solar module manufacturer Thornova Solar and Nextpower, a provider of advanced solar tracker and structural solutions, marked a milestone in their growing strategic cooperation with the signing of a Master Supply Agreement (MSA).

The agreement, confirmed at RE+ 2026, further strengthens the collaboration between the two companies, combining Thornova Solar’s U.S.-made solar modules with Nextpower’s U.S.-manufactured steel frame technology. The expanded effort is designed to deliver increased domestic content opportunities and enhanced structural performance, providing greater value to customers developing utility-scale and commercial and industrial (C&I) solar projects across the United States.

According to the companies, integrating advanced steel frame solutions into selected Thornova Solar module series addresses two increasingly crucial priorities in the U.S. solar market: maximizing domestic content and improving module resilience under demanding environmental conditions.

The combined solution offers several key benefits:.

Industry observers note that the solution is particularly relevant for projects in demanding U.S. environments, including high-wind regions across the Midwest and Southeast, where structural reliability and long-term module performance are critical considerations.

Industry observers note that “The signing of this Master Supply Agreement represents an important step in strengthening our relationship with Nextpower and expanding the value we deliver to U.S. customers,” noted Andrea Bodenhagen, global marketing director of Thornova Solar. “By bringing together U.S.-made solar modules and domestically manufactured steel frame technology, we are helping our customers increase domestic content while benefiting from stronger, more resilient module solutions. This is exactly the kind of collaboration needed to advance a competitive U.S. solar manufacturing ecosystem.”.

Industry observers note that “We’re excited to deepen our strategic collaboration with Thornova and bring modules featuring Nextpower’s domestically manufactured steel frames to the U.S. market,” mentioned Jenya Meydbray, vice president and general manager of Nextpower. “NX CoreFrame offers a significant opportunity to advance module strength and reliability, addressing industry challenges such as glass breakage and demanding environmental loads while delivering greater confidence to solar developers and owners.”.

It has been revealed that the MSA reflects the shared commitment of both companies to strengthening domestic manufacturing and delivering solutions that respond to the evolving technical and commercial requirements of the U.S. solar market.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

COP31 climate talks break down shows that fossil fuel interests remain a major obstacle to climate action.

The lack of a final text at the end of COP31 reveals how far the fossil fuel industry is willing to go to keep its polluting businesses operating, states T&E. While the final text of COP28, in 2023, called for ‘transitioning away from fossil fuels in the energy system’, fossil-producing countries have blocked similar language in subsequent COPs despite the growing economic and social costs of climate change.

Antony Froggatt, senior director at T&E, remarked: “In a year marked by record oil prices and extreme temperatures, fossil fuel companies moved to block any agreement calling for a phase-out of oil, gas, and coal. They did so to protect their commercial interests even as solar and wind already power the majority of the grid in countries worldwide, and electric vehicles make up nearly half of new car sales in the world’s largest auto market.”.

This is not the end of the international processes, and the Paris Agreement remains in place. The next COP will take place in Ethiopia, and the phase-out of fossil fuels will once again be discussed. In the meantime, the Santa Marta process, which grew out of COP30’s failure to agree on a fossil fuel roadmap, will once again meet, and it is expected that countries representing one-third of the world’s economy will debate and develop practical ways to move away from coal, oil and gas.

Analysis by T&E at the beginning of the week highlights that EVs displace five times more oil globally than they did five years ago. Battery-electric vehicles already displace 1.2 million barrels of oil a day and avoid more than 200 Mt of CO2-equivalent a year.

“Petrostates’ chokehold on COP31 underscores the need for the progressive majority to continue pushing for international co-operation and global targets on electrification that can accelerate decarbonisation while improving energy security, air quality and economic prosperity,” added Antony Froggatt.

Recent findings suggest that “The same oil shock that delivered record profits for the oil industry has pushed up costs for the world’s most vulnerable countries, most of which import their fuel. Governments should make the polluter pay. Excess profits should be heavily taxed, and the revenue used to fund electrification and climate resilience where it is needed most,” he concludes.

Parking lots should be legally required to display a sign that notes "Enter at your own peril." If not so much for the property's legal nightmare, but rather for the dangerous events that typically unfold on these concrete or paved wastelands for cars. Why be afraid though when you could be like the Brits and turn a parking lot into a professional frenzy championship?

The annual competition is called the Ken Wharton Autotest. Held by the Hagley & District Light Car Club, it's somewhat reminiscent of a 16-year-old's driver test, just on super steroids. According to the 2026 competition's video summary on YouTube, competitors in small cars like Mini Coopers, lightweight sports cars, and specially modified machines are "built to change direction quickly. Outright power matters less than agility, grip and the driver's ability to put the car exactly where it needs to be." Basically, imagine Ken Block and Travis Pastrana Gymkhana performances — as a rapid time trial.

Ashley Lamont, is one of these competitors, whose absolutely near-flawless run was shared to YouTube just days ago. Lamont whipped his bright green-liveried Caterham seamlessly about the entire course in 71.3 seconds, which helped his team of Northern Ireland clinch the win for the 2026 competition.

According to recent reports, the racing competition displays a combination of motorkhana, gymkhana and American-style autocross through a competitive field set up with cones. Drivers are required to memorize the course and where their car needs to be at every turn while rapidly throwing the car from forward to reverse, back and forth (that poor transmission!) It's a timed trial as well, so the driver has to complete it as fast as possible. The fastest team can win the competition, but consistency really matters in this as well. It's mesmerizing to watch.

Sources indicate that what that means for the audience is a wildly disorienting scene of a car being whipped around a fairly vague-looking circuit like the most eloquently-executed choreographed dance as the driver pulls 180s and J-turns without blinking. At the end of each run, you almost want them to get out of the car to take a bow after such a performance. What's unique about Lamont's run is his movement, compared to other competing drivers who sometimes pause ever so briefly before the next move, Lamont drives from flow state to flow state.

By the end, I honestly don't know who to be more impressed with, the driver, or the camera man capable of zooming in and following these cars' every move.

The 2026 Manhattan Wealth Rush: Ultraluxury Real Estate Is Smashing Sales Records

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1163 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Manhattan luxury market has had a banner year despite the pied-à-terre tax and the recent stock market correction.
  • Trophy properties—those priced $10 million and above—made up half the contracts signed last week, leading the luxury market into the second biggest year in two decades, according to Olshan Realty.
  • 22, an impressive 294 contracts were signed at $10 million and above, not far off the peak year of 2021, when 400 were signed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Manhattan luxury market has had a banner year despite the pied-à-terre tax and the recent stock market correction.

Trophy properties—those priced $10 million and above—made up half the contracts signed last week, leading the luxury market into the second biggest year in two decades, according to Olshan Realty.

As of Nov. 22, an impressive 294 contracts were signed at $10 million and above, not far off the peak year of 2021, when 400 were signed. The average asking price for last week was $10.5 million, and properties were moving with a fairly low 5% average discount.

Corcoran's Deborah Grubman, who co-listed last week's most expensive sale—a $28.75 million triplex in the Pritzker Prize–winning Richard Meier building in the West Village—says that the luxury market normally indicates signs of slowing down around the Thanksgiving holiday. But not this year.

"New York is still a very desirable destination for people of wealth," she tells Realtor.com®.

The glass triplex at 176 Perry St.—one of the city's most coveted blocks—was owned by Broadway and movie star Hugh Jackman. The condo, built in 2001, had been on and off the market since June 2022, and at one point was priced at $39 million.

Jackman and his ex-wife, Deborra-Lee Furness, purchased the 11,000-square-foot minimalist abode for $21 million in 2008. Spanning the eighth, ninth and 10th floors, it is "one of the most dramatic apartments in Manhattan," the listing states.

According to recent reports, the full-service condominium comes with sweeping views of the river and Hudson River Park and is within walking distance of The High Line, Little Island, the Meatpacking District, Bleecker Steet, and the Whitney Museum. Jean-Georges Vongerichten's Perry Street Restaurant is on its ground floor.

The Richard Meier building, one of the first ultraluxe buildings that far west, helped change the face of the once-gritty area.

It has been revealed that "It was the first 'star-chitect' building in the West Village on the waterfront," states the broker. "It was groundbreaking in terms of luxury. At the time, people said, 'Who is going to live in the highway?' It predated all that green space.".

While it took Jackman about five years to unload the property, Grubman says that the West Village—and Perry Street, which stretches from Greenwich Avenue to the river—remains in high demand.

Recent findings suggest that "It's a street that's got lots of charm and history," she says. "The West Village is out of central casting. You still have the charm of the small townhouses and tree-lined streets.

"The only thing that's really changed a lot is the price point.".

Michelle Griffith of Douglas Elliman represented the buyer of one of the year's top sales: a $16.5 million, 3,855-square-foot condo in the Waldorf Astoria Residences at 301 Park Ave. in Midtown.

The luxury broker says her trophy property sales for 2026 are on track to beat her previous best year, which was 2021.

That year, when 400 ultraluxe contracts were signed, those who weren't fleeing lockdowns were shelling out for multimillion-dollar properties, spurred on by historically low interest rates in the 2% to 4% range.

Today, with higher rates hovering around 7%, there are plenty of cash-flush buyers snapping up ultraluxe homes. (Some still prefer 7% mortgage rates to pulling their money out of more lucrative investments.).

"The phrase that sums up 2026 for me is 'bidding wars,'" the broker tells Realtor.com. "This year will go down as my best year.".

She attributes the surging high-end market to a couple of factors: tight inventory pushing up prices and sparking intense competition, and the "insanely high and insanely competitive" rental market, with rents double or triple what they were just a few years ago.

According to Realtor.com, a three-bedroom-plus in Manhattan has a median monthly rent of $5,375, an increase of 35.6% over the past seven years, requiring a household to earn $215,000 a year just to stay afloat with rent.

According to recent reports, however, those who want a luxury three-bedroom-plus abode in a trendy neighborhood can shell out significantly more. Griffith says that a few years ago, a large luxury dwelling in an area like Tribeca could cost around $19,000 a month. But now?

It has been revealed that "It would work itself up close to $30,000," she notes. "So those people are saying, 'Do I want to spend $30,000 a month or should I pivot and think about buying something? How much am I going to overspend before I say, 'OK, let me buy'?".

Combine stratospheric rents with "inventory levels down across the board," and prices have skyrocketed.

"If you have something good in the West Village, in Tribeca, on the Upper East Side, it is likely going to trade itself up in a bidding war," claims the agent.

When dream turnkey apartments began to disappear from listings, buyers became more willing to take on projects, resulting in a stronger-than-normal luxury co-op market. In general, co-ops are much older—and cheaper—than condos.

In a recent development, while the week ending Nov. 22 saw luxury condos outpace co-ops 18-4, there have been several weeks during 2026 when that gap was considerably narrower—and one week in June when co-ops won out.

Recent findings suggest that "These are places that might require several million dollars to renovate," claims Griffith. "And now that market too is getting absorbed.".

According to recent reports, she states those who didn't leave the city during the COVID-19 pandemic—fleeing to Westchester, Connecticut, or Florida—are the die-hards who are committed to the city long term. And they are the ones out there bidding up and buying.

Especially relevant are families whose children are deep in the school system.

"They're putting down roots for a minimum of 10 to 15 years," she indicates.

Despite her banner year, Griffith claims she isn't planning a celebration just yet. Next year could be a different story as the pied-à-terre surcharge ramps up to replace Department of Finance valuations with significantly higher "fair market" valuations for 2029.

In a recent development, "This year was an emotional journey," she claims. "There were many bidding wars we won, but also many we lost. I'm the type who focuses more on, 'What are the deals that we lost?'".

Industry observers note that the second-highest contract of the week was a $25 million sponsor duplex penthouse at 133 E. 73rd St. Listing agency Modlin Group did not return a request for more information.
