#99418. What Are The Different Classes Of Campers, RVs, And Motorhomes?

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2047 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

What Are The Different Classes Of Campers, RVs, And Motorhomes?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2047 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There is a wealth of choices when it comes to the types of campers, RVs, and motorhomes you can spend your free time in, so much so that you can find one of them for just about any style of camping and almost any budget.
  • It also helps to understand the different classes and types of RVs, motorhomes, and campers.
  • Next, you have towables — campers that are towed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is a wealth of choices when it comes to the types of campers, RVs, and motorhomes you can spend your free time in, so much so that you can find one of them for just about any style of camping and almost any budget. They range from small pull-behinds that aren't much more than a step up from a tent to those mammoth rolling McMansions you see plodding along the interstate. With so many choices, how do you know which one is right for you? One place to start is our list of five things to know before you buy a used RV.

It also helps to understand the different classes and types of RVs, motorhomes, and campers. "RV" is a general term for all campers and motorhomes. "Motorhomes" refer to RVs that you can drive. There are three classes of motorhomes: Class A, Class B, and Class C. Class A motorhomes are the largest, Class B are the smallest, and Class C is in between, with some overlap in size with the other classes.

Next, you have towables — campers that are towed. This includes large travel trailers — which utilize a ball hitch linked to the towing vehicle's frame or rear bumper — bigger fifth-wheels attaching to a hitch over the truck's rear axle, and foldable campers like pop-ups and A-frames. Even though they don't have a drivetrain, slide-in truck campers aren't technically towables since they're hauled. You also have hybrid campers expanding out to the sides and rear, as well as park models, which aren't meant to do much traveling, but are designed to be towed to a spot and left there as a resort unit.

If you've ever done an interstate road trip, you've passed more than one of those behemoth RVs, usually driven by some retiree taking their time in the slow lane. The really significant RVs that look like a bus are Class A motorhomes. Thor Industries indicates that this class can range from approximately 25 to 45 feet in length and weigh from around 12,500 to 54,000 pounds. You'll also find a maximum of four slide-outs and room to sleep up to ten people, which, frankly, is more than we could comfortably put up in our house. Some of these bad boys have a loft and a patio on the back. The Thor Aria 4000 is particularly posh, offering a spacious master bedroom, a set of bunk beds, a full stack washer and dryer, four spots for TVs (including one on the outside), and two full bathrooms — one of which has two sinks. Then you have Class A toy haulers, featuring a garage that can carry an ATV or motorcycles.

Industry observers note that since Class As often have all the comforts of home, it makes sense why some luxury models can cost as much as houses in nice neighborhoods. The Newmar King Aire, for instance, is listed at over $1.7 million. Granted, that's the tech giant's top-of-the-line luxury model. The least expensive Class A it offers, presumably for the poors, lists at over $250,000. Many Class A motorhomes are built on a commercial bus or truck chassis, and usually have a flat front end. You can find them in either gas or diesel.

It has been revealed that if you can bear to go camping without loading up everything from your house, or if you'd like to stay the night somewhere without taking up the entire back parking lot of a Cracker Barrel, then maybe Class B motorhomes are for you. They are much smaller than Class A motorhomes, usually around 17 to 24 feet in length, and weigh around 8,550 to 11,000-plus pounds, though these ranges can vary based on whom you ask. Thor indicates Class B motorhomes can sleep up to four people. Maybe. When it comes to the ones we've seen, sleeping four people would be pretty tight.

Industry observers note that that's not to say some models can't be fancy. The VACANZA-ion 22 comes with an impressive galley that includes a combination microwave-convection-air fryer and a nicely sized refrigerator-freezer. It also comes with AWD and a power awning with a wind sensor.

Industry observers note that these RVs are also called campervans, and are typically built on a Mercedes-Benz Sprinter, Ford Transit, or Ram ProMaster chassis. Still, these are not the same as the vans that vanlifers on YouTube build out. Class B RVs are sold new, completely self-contained, with a bedroom, kitchen, bathroom, and running water. The vehicles DIY vanlifers usually start with are regular cargo vans that they've stuck a bed, a sink, and often a bucket into. Some of them aren't even tall enough to stand up in. In certain cases, buying a van like a Ford Transit and converting it won't save any money.

So, if Class B motorhomes are smaller than Class A, then Class Cs must be smaller than Class B, right? Ha ha, no, that would be too logical. Class C motorhomes fit in between, not as big as Class A RVs, but larger than Class B RVs. If the three bears each owned RVs, Goldilocks would probably find the Class C to be just right. Class C RVs are built on cutaway truck or van chassis and usually have a sleeping compartment over the cab. The elements combine to form a distinctive silhouette. Thor indicates Class Cs run from 23 to 39 feet long and weigh about 11,000 to 32,700 pounds. As you can see, there can be some overlap in size between Class C and Class A motorhomes.

According to recent reports, some RVs are given the designation "Super C," but that's a marketing category, not an official class. Each manufacturer has a different definition of what a Super C is, but what they have in common is that they are essentially really large Class C motorhomes, usually on a medium- or heavy-duty commercial truck chassis. One example is the Entegra Coach Accolade. Depending on the floorplan, you could have an electric fireplace, as well as a full-size couch and a full-size dinette, not a dinette that doubles as a couch.

Sources indicate that it's much the same with the term "B+," which is used to describe smaller Class C motorhomes that look like large Class B RVs, since they often lack the overhead compartment. They are still Class C RVs, though, because they are built on a cutaway van or chassis.

Recent findings suggest that most regular readers of Jalopnik know what a fifth-wheel is. We are a car website, after all. In case you don't know, a fifth wheel is a large hitch for big trailers. You've seen a semi-truck without its trailer. That big horseshoe-looking thing on the back of it is the fifth wheel. Fifth wheels can also be installed in the beds of heavy-duty pickups, and the hitch can connect with fifth-wheel RV trailers, which tend to be pretty large.

According to recent reports, while this references Thor's own lineup rather than a broader industry range like the previous examples, Thor says fifth-wheel trailers measure from 36 to 45 feet long. That means they can have more living space than even a Class A motorhome, especially if you consider the compartment that comes out over the hitch. Some of these trailers are massive enough to be toy haulers, as well.

According to recent reports, but living space isn't the only advantage of a fifth wheel over a motorhome. Imagine you've backed, with great difficulty, into your camp spot, set up the chairs, grill, outside lights, mat, and other items. You rolled out the awning. Then it occurred to you that you forgot to pack plastic silverware. It's just one item, but how are you supposed to eat dinner without forks? With a fifth wheel, you don't have to pack everything back up and break down your site just to go to the store. You can just disconnect your truck, leave your trailer at the site, and go.

You don't necessarily need a massive dually equipped with a fifth wheel to pull a camper around. Conventional travel trailers are made to be towed with a standard receiver hitch (frame-mounted receiver) attached to the back of an SUV or pickup, most commonly full-size. Some campers are light enough to be towed by a small car. Honda recently built a prototype of a trailer designed to be towed by EVs and small crossovers. Of course, you'll always want to check the towing capacity of your vehicle against the weight of a fully-loaded camper before trying to pull one. Travel trailers can range in size from around 15 feet all the way to over 40 feet. They can weigh as little as a couple thousand pounds or as much as nearly 14,000 pounds.

According to recent reports, the biggest ones have pretty much everything a fifth wheel has, except for the sleeping compartment that would go over a fifth wheel hitch. The smaller and mid-size travel trailers can come in a variety of shapes. You might be familiar with the small teardrop trailers. Some teardrop trailers may contain a kitchenette and a wet bath, while the smallest ones don't even have enough room to stand up in. Still, it's better than sleeping in a tent.

Prices vary wildly. Runaway Campers sells a tiny pull-behind, the CoolCamp, for just over $6,000. The 28-foot Airstream Trade Wind 27 FB is probably mid-size for a travel trailer, but is not mid-priced at almost $163,000. The 36-foot Prowler 3202DSB starts at around $42,000.

Sources indicate that if you'd like a camper that's lighter than a small conventional travel trailer, is easier to maneuver, and doesn't take up as much storage space (yet often has more room than a typical teardrop), you might look into pop-up campers. These campers stay folded down into a very compact trailer while they are stored or are being towed, and then fold out into a nice-sized living space at the campsite.

Traditional pop-up campers additionally extend their ends, providing two separate sleeping areas. These are soft-sided sections, meaning the experience is sort of like being in a tent, but without sleeping on the ground. Pop-up campers can come equipped with a simple toilet, shower, sink, and sometimes even air conditioning. However, basic ones lack amenities like a bathroom.

According to recent reports, another type of folding camper is the hard-sided A-frame. The roofs on these campers fold out to a point, resembling an "A", and can feel smaller than pop-ups, though they sometimes have the same amenities. Others are very simple, being just one step above a tent. Hybrid campers are a little different. Generally, they do not fold down, but they do pop out on the ends to provide more space.

In a recent development, if you've ever watched "Doctor Who," you know that the hero travels around space and time in a machine they call Tardis. On the outside, Tardis looks like a 1960s-era police call box you'd find in the U.K., but on the inside, it was a huge, multi-room ship. That's sort of the sensation you get stepping into some truck campers — they seem a lot bigger on the inside than they look on the outside, so much so that you might forget you're standing in the back of your pickup. You should take a look at the Host Cascade to see what we mean. This thing can come with, depending on your chosen floor blueprint, two recliners, a sectional couch and dinette, a sizable kitchenette, a dry bath with a full shower, a bedroom, and even a simulated fireplace that is actually an electric heater. We don't mean to gatekeep, but at what point does camping stop being camping and just become staying in another house?

Industry observers note that there are simpler truck campers, of course, and most are, in fact, much more modest. A dinette, a sink and stove counter, a bathroom, and a bed compartment are pretty standard for most slide-in truck campers. Some are even simpler, with a pop-up soft-side roof, a bed platform, and maybe some benches. What all of these different RV classes and types boil down to is that you've got plenty of camping choices.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, ahmedabad, India — Adani Cement, part of the Adani Portfolio and one of India’s leading building materials solutions providers, flagged off Heavy-Duty Electric Trucks at its Sanghi Plant in Gujarat. This is the first-ever deployment of EV trucks by Adani Cement and a defining milestone in the manufacturer’s sustainability and green logistics journey.

Industry observers note that mr. Vinod Bahety, CEO of Cement Business, Adani Group, said, “The deployment at Sanghi is just the beginning. We have identified multiple routes across India for EV-based transport of clinker and cement. Every truck we electrify reduces our carbon footprint and insulates our logistics cost base from diesel price volatility. This is smart sustainability—it benefits the people, the planet, and the balance sheet. This is our commitment in action—to build a greener, more competitive cement manufacturer that serves India’s growth while protecting its future.”.

Industry observers note that the economic case for heavy-duty EV trucks in India’s cement sector has reached a structural tipping point. Over the past decade, diesel prices rose 60%, while Li-ion battery pack costs fell by approximately 70% and solar tariffs declined 47%.

Diesel trucks emit approximately 0.7375 kg CO₂ per km and when powered by renewable energy, EV trucks can eliminate up to 100% of these freight emissions, making logistics electrification a powerful lever for Scope 3 decarbonization. Adani Cement’s 410-truck fleet is projected to reduce over 25,000 tonnes of CO₂ annually, displacing the equivalent of 11 million litres of diesel per year, with plans to expand across additional routes and plants.

India is the world’s second-largest cement producer, and the movement of limestone, clinker, and finished cement across vast supply chains is an essential, but carbon-intensive, part of the sector’s operations. Adani Cement’s EV fleet deployment addresses both the cost and climate dimensions of this challenge directly.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to Kathryn McCallum, the director of strategy at the Climate Action Network Australia, there were 624 delegates from the 14 Pacificc Small Island Developing States at the conference in Turkey this month and 700 paid lobbyists for the carbon capture industry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

COP31, the annual UN climate conference that took place this month, ended on a sour note after negotiators were unable to reach an agreement to include language calling for a transition away from fossil fuels in the final communiqué  — language that was included two years ago at the conclusion of COP 29 in Dubai.

How is it possible to explain such backsliding at a time when a Kelvin wave — a wall of unusually hot water — is impacting the coast of every country along the eastern edge of the Pacific Ocean? Authorities say unusually high temperatures all across Europe led to the premature death of more than 50,000 people last summer. In addition, huge swaths of the Earth’s land mass are experiencing either severe drought or punishing floods. How can anybody ignore the events happening before their very eyes?

You know the answer — MONEY! According to Kathryn McCallum, the director of strategy at the Climate Action Network Australia, there were 624 delegates from the 14 Pacificc Small Island Developing States at the conference in Turkey this month and 700 paid lobbyists for the carbon capture industry. In an email to CleanTechnica, she stated,.

“There is no public momentum from parties in the COP31 process asking for carbon capture, utilization and storage, yet it is in the final draft text. As a result, in the coming hours, parties at COP31 will decide whether to lock in a [methane] fired future with a rapid scale-up of carbon dumping. The potential inclusion of a huge increase in global carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS) would be one of the biggest loopholes for the fossil fuel industry ever to be included in a COP text. Climate advocates are highly alarmed and are urging parties to come to their senses and make decisions that advance global climate action rather than the interests of the gas industry.”.

Industry observers note that as it turns out, the knife in the back delivered by fossil fuel interests at COP31 was too much for negotiators from the EU and the UK to swallow. According to reNEWS, the European Union expressed its “profound disappointment” with the draft cover decision following the close of the COP31 conference.

“At a point where the world urgently needs action to avert disastrous level of global warming, the draft cover decision falls short,” a joint EU statement read. “We will not endorse a cover decision that does not respond to the science, that disregards the implementation gap, and risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required to correct the overshoot and bring 1.5°C within reach. We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change.”.

The statement listed a number on other concerns with the draft cover decision, including that the draft extols carbon capture, usage, and storage technologies “disproportionally” as a method to deal with the climate crisis. This is magical thinking, the statement by the EU noted.

The UK also refused to be sucked in by the absurd claims that carbon capture was a plausible alternative to reducing the world’s reliance on fossil fuels. The Independent reports that UK energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh expressed regret that the talks had failed to produce the “bold ambition” needed, as the negotiations became mired in disagreement over a draft agreement that contained no mention of fossil fuels.

Sources indicate that the UK formally objected to a proposed deal that “moves us backwards on the science” of tackling climate change. In a statement, Fahnbulleh remarked, “This COP sought to confront hard truths — that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with ever more urgency to address it. The moment required bold ambition and we have been working tirelessly to try to build consensus. It is immensely disappointing we have been unable to do so.”.

There are a number of ways to remediate the emissions from burning fossil fuels, which are nothing more than stored sunshine from millions of years ago. We could irradiate them with unicorn farts, incinerate them in nuclear fusion facilities, are store them in the basement at Mar-A-Loco, where large quantities of toxic fumes are already present. There is only one problem — none of those solutions work. In fact, the only thing that does work is burning less fossil fuels, until we are able to phase them out entirely.

Industry observers note that in  2025, Mark Jacobson, a professor of civil and environmental engineering at Stanford University, and his colleagues, published a research paper in the journal Environmental Science and Technology. In it he wrote that if the nations of the world transitioned to renewable energy — solar, wind, and hydroelectric power — they would eliminate energy-related air pollution deaths and CO2-equivalent emissions while reducing their energy needs by 54.4 percent, annual energy costs by 59.6 percent, and annual social costs — energy, plus health, plus climate — by 91.8 percent. Who wouldn’t want that?

On the other hand, Jacobson and his team wrote that every dollar spent on carbon capture instead of wind, water, and solar, “increases carbon dioxide pollution, energy requirements, energy costs, pipelines, and total social costs.” This holds true even if zero-emission energy systems power the technology deployed to extract carbon dioxide. “It’s always an opportunity cost to use clean, renewable energy for direct air capture instead of replacing a fossil fuel CO2 source, just like it’s an opportunity cost to use it for AI or bitcoin mining. You’re preventing renewables from replacing fossil fuel sources because you’re creating more demand for those renewables,” he mentioned.

In a recent development, “Opportunity costs” is the operative concept here. If you are in Peoria, you cannot be in Philadelphia. If you spend $10.00 on pretzels, you cannot spend it on vegetables. If you buy a new car, you cannot use that money to go to Cabo San Lucas. The money the world pisses away on carbon capture cannot be used to build solar, wind, and hydro resources. It’s as simple as that.

The take away here is that fossil fuels will always win the policy debate. So what will drive the transition to renewable energy? Lower prices for renewables and eliminating concerns about energy insecurity from geopolitical disruptions like the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Low prices always win and people are pretty sick and tired of paying six bucks for diesel while watching the cost of electricity soar higher and higher.

Sources indicate that “The first one now shall later be last,” Bob Dylan taught us. That’s a message of hope inside the carbon dioxide cloud the fossil fuel industry has gifted us. The only question is whether the transition will happen soon enough to avoid a climate catastrophe. It’s hard to imagine destroying a planet and decimating your customer base is a good long term business strategy, but that’s what the executives in charge of the world’s oil, methane, and coal industries seem to think makes for good business. There are none so blind as those who will not see.

At $28,850, Is This Classic 1989 Range Rover Still A Bargain?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that james May, the former television presenter and current gin hawker, has just bought himself an old Range Rover.
  • James May's former compatriot, Jeremy Clarkson, complained in a 2014 Top Gear magazine review that the BMW M3 (actually, M4, but let's not get pedantic) was too twitchy on the track.
  • It has been revealed that happily for us, the 2006 BMW M3 we looked at on Monday was one of the last to be mostly analog.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that james May, the former television presenter and current gin hawker, has just bought himself an old Range Rover. While he's not exactly what we'd call a trendsetter, today's Nice Price or No Dice Range Rover Classic may be alluring enough to make May jealous.

James May's former compatriot, Jeremy Clarkson, complained in a 2014 Top Gear magazine review that the BMW M3 (actually, M4, but let's not get pedantic) was too twitchy on the track. Jezza deduced that the problem lay in the car's fancy electric power steering not being as communicative or as quick as its hydraulic predecessors.

It has been revealed that happily for us, the 2006 BMW M3 we looked at on Monday was one of the last to be mostly analog. With low mileage and a great color, our M3 likely might have even earned Clarkson's approval. Unfortunately for its seller, the set $22,000 asking price did not get the approval of enough of you to carry the day. That was obvious in the 62% 'No Dice' loss it suffered.

According to recent reports, while the Range Rover name has become synonymous with high-end luxury off-roading, that wasn't always the case, nor was it the model's potential name. Land Rover long intended to build something more refined and civilized than its namesake hair-shirt-on-wheels, jeep-like truck introduced shortly after WWII. Back then, the internal code name for the envisioned more car-like truck was "Road Rover," with development beginning as far back as 1957.

In a recent development, that Road Rover evolved into Range Rover, introduced in 1971 and carrying the Rover (nee Buick) all-alloy V8 and coil springs in place of the Land Rover's leaves, wrapped in a clean, simple alloy-and-steel body. Rover intended to sell the Range Rover in the U.S. from the get-go, but financial turmoil at the manufacturer and its parent, British Leyland, quashed those looks. It took over a decade and a half for the company to get its ducks in a row, allowing North American sales to begin in 1987.

Sources indicate that when it debuted in North America, the fancy-pants Range Rover sold like hotcakes, though, in typical British Leyland fashion, quality-control and service complications tainted the ownership experience for many buyers. As a result, many used, off-warranty models tanked in value over the years. As we will see, that may not be the case anymore.

This 1989 Range Rover is the original short-wheelbase edition, powered by a 3.9-liter Lucas fuel-injected version of the long-running V8. In this model year, that was good for 178 horsepower and 298 pound-feet of torque, according to factory specifications. Behind that is a ZF-sourced four-speed automatic and Borg Warner two-speed transfer case. Stout live axles sit at both ends, and the coil-sprung suspension offers plenty of travel.

According to the ad, this 83,232-mile Range Rover has been "Fully Restored" and is described as "AMAZING Super Cool.".

Sources indicate that that restoration must have been fairly light in nature since there is evidence of some shortcuts having been taken. That's most obvious in the driver's seat leather, which has a large swath of dye attempting to mask (unsuccessfully) some crazing in the side bolster. Other issues include lumpy carpeting and a torn parking brake boot.

Aside from those minor challenges, the interior appears to be in good condition and features what the seller describes as a "High dollar Custom Audio/Video system.".

While the interior might have some demerits, there's nothing to complain about on the exterior. The white paint is clean and unmarred and is a color that is both popular and goes with anything. That white hue extends to the Range Rover's iconic three-spoke alloy wheels. Those might be better served by the original gun-metal finish, but that's subjective and irrelevant to our purposes. Other things to note: the bodywork has been drilled and capped on each corner outside of the light clusters, likely at one time for the fitting of brush guards. Also, the body has been entirely denuded of badges, save for the center caps on the wheels.

We aren't given any information about the truck's mechanical history, or any photos of the engine bay, although the seller assures us that it "Runs/Drives excellent with great power and perfect gearing all around," additionally saying that it has been "Loved and maintained and it indicates!!".

The original Range Rover has entered the stage of life where it can be considered a classic, with those for sale being either cheap, absolute money-pit fright pigs or updated, restored pride-of-ownership examples like this one. Interestingly, Porsche's 928 falls in the same boat.

Recent findings suggest that it is advised that any ridiculously cheap Range Rover should almost always be avoided at all costs. Bringing such a dog back from the brink would likely be a fool's errand, quickly emptying bank accounts in the process.

Industry observers note that for anyone wanting to get into the classic Range Rover scene, it's probably best to pay the piper up front and get the best one money can buy. Is this clean-title claimed restored edition the best? No, but then it's probably good enough. We need to determine whether "good enough" is good enough to command the $28,850 the seller is asking. It should be noted that spectacular examples—those with re-trimmed cabins, better colors, and maybe a displacement bump for the engine—do tend to go for half again as much as this.

In a recent development, still, it's a shock to see original Range Rovers asking so much after years of values being in the doldrums. What's your take on this restored Range Rover and that $28,850 price tag? Does that feel market-fair given the model's age and status? Or is that just crazy talk?

Los Angeles, California, Craigslist, or go here if the ad disappears.

Industry News: The European Competitiveness Fund, the Backbone of a Modern European Investment Policy

💡 Key Takeaways
  • European businesses call for a robust, well-funded European Competitiveness Fund.
  • Europe is losing ground in technological leadership and struggles to scale strategic technologies, while volatile energy costs and external dependencies continue to dampen business confidence.
  • Europe’s path to enduring technological leadership relies on our ability to scale strategic technologies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

European businesses call for a robust, well-funded European Competitiveness Fund.

Dear Chancellors, Prime Ministers, Presidents,.

Europe is losing ground in technological leadership and struggles to scale strategic technologies, while volatile energy costs and external dependencies continue to dampen business confidence.

Europe’s path to enduring technological leadership relies on our ability to scale strategic technologies. By stabilising energy costs, providing a path to clean industrial renewal and cultivating European resilience, we are laying the groundwork for robust business and investors’ confidence. Public investment has a crucial role to play to address these vital challenges. We require a smarter, more strategic investment policy for Europe.

Recent findings suggest that we, more than 75 undersigned businesses, call on European leaders to agree to a Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) commensurate with Europe’s challenges, to protect its investment capacity and place long-term productivity growth, resilience and decarbonisation at its core. We believe the European Competitiveness Fund (ECF) represents a step-change in the EU’s investment policy and must be strengthened in the remaining negotiations.

The ECF with its toolbox projects the ambition to provide tailored support to the investment and scale-up challenge Europe faces. This is a positive evolution of the EU funding landscape. With a bigger role for the EU’s derisking instrument InvestEU, the ECF can become Europe’s modern investment vehicle with an increased use of guarantees, loans and equity to unlock strategic investments.

According to recent reports, at the same time, non-repayable support needs to be dedicated to scaling up sectors that deliver high strategic value but cannot yet secure commercial capital in Europe. Ramp-up support for Europe’s cleantech manufacturing, including support for OpEx, is needed to make Europe’s bid to regain technological leadership credible.

According to recent reports, the advisory services for SMEs and the single access portal promises a simpler access to funding for firms across Europe. If successful, the ECF can pool additional national funds through merit-based procedures open to eligible projects across the single market to bring further alignment and synergies into European industrial development.

Recent findings suggest that europe’s energy import dependency has become a strategic vulnerability for European businesses. To increase our economic resilience, the EU must prioritise investments into energy sovereignty. Incentives need to pivot capital allocation away from fossil fuel infrastructure, and towards clean energy and electrification. From 2028, the next MFF should not support upcoming fossil-fuel infrastructure that prolongs dependency on fossil fuels, while providing narrowly defined safeguards for security of supply. We need steering mechanisms to reduce fossil fuel dependencies. EU funding can help to tackle high upfront costs and derisk the switch to cleaner and more reliable energy. Otherwise, long investment cycles create severe fossil fuel lock-in effects that threaten our operational autonomy with increasingly volatile fossil energy prices.

Europe’s investment gap cannot be solved by a smarter, more strategic funding approach alone. The confidence into European competitiveness needs to translate into a sizable budget for the clean transition to have lasting impact. The Commission proposes an average annual budget of €3.3 billion for a clean transition and industrial decarbonisation window of the ECF. This number is dwarfed by recurring estimates of the annual climate investment deficit of €344 billion. At the same time, according to the OECD, industrial subsidies have reached the highest levels since the financial crisis 2008.

Sources indicate that we urge European leaders to respond to the evolving investment environment and adopt the European Parliament’s proposal to increase the size of the ECF by €26.6 billion and to allocate a substantial share of the additional funding for industrial decarbonisation and clean transition. The more efficient use of financial instruments and a strategic prioritisation can improve the impact of EU funding but cannot substitute the investment needs Europe is facing to boost competitiveness and security.

The next long-term budget and the European Competitiveness Fund must become the investment trigger for European businesses to regain competitiveness at the global scale, based on clear incentives and regulatory certainty. We businesses urge leaders to demonstrate a long-term vision and make the ECF the cornerstone of a new EU green industrial strategy.

#99412. Breaking: Steel solar panel frames hit the mainstream

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1371 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Solarpowerworldonline ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Steel solar panel frames hit the mainstream

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1371 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Solarpowerworldonline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that steel is considered the backbone of the American economy, critical for both national and economic security.
  • In a recent development, A factory worker places a section of steel solar panel frames on a pallet in Welser Profile’s plant in Valley City, Ohio.
  • Recent findings suggest that roll-form steel company Welser Profile began manufacturing Nextpower’s NX CoreFrame steel panel frames earlier this year at its facility in Valley City, Ohio, just 30 miles outside Cleveland, and Solar Power World was invited to view production of its first major orders before adding another line fully dedicated to the solar component before the end of the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that steel is considered the backbone of the American economy, critical for both national and economic security. It’s also the backbone of solar power construction, found commonly in the racking and mounting structures tilting solar panels toward the sun. And now, after years of tests and trials, an Ohio factory is roll-forming steel for a solar product that could use a stronger backbone — the solar panel.

In a recent development, A factory worker places a section of steel solar panel frames on a pallet in Welser Profile’s plant in Valley City, Ohio. Credit: Nextpower.

Recent findings suggest that roll-form steel company Welser Profile began manufacturing Nextpower’s NX CoreFrame steel panel frames earlier this year at its facility in Valley City, Ohio, just 30 miles outside Cleveland, and Solar Power World was invited to view production of its first major orders before adding another line fully dedicated to the solar component before the end of the year. Module frame company Origami Solar originally had the idea that swapping aluminum frames with steel would not only save the solar industry money and cut back on carbon emissions, it would also provide more physical support to bigger and heavier solar panels.

Welser, an Austrian organization with origins dating back to the 1660s, is a leader in roll-form steel profiles typically only seen in aluminum extrusions and helped produce a steel frame that’s easy for panel manufacturers to assemble and contractors to handle.

“What’s special about Welser Profile is we pre-notch features in the material before it gets formed,” said Bill Johnson, North America CEO of Welser Profile. “Everything about the solar industry is about how do we make it more efficient, cheaper, faster, better? You do that by all these little details to add value farther up the stream that minimizes labor, install cost. Our hole patterns and other features allow operators to snap things together, not bolt or weld things. Everyone is looking at how to make this work in a Lego setup, not a high-intense labor workforce installing all these panels.”.

Welser is helping bring the Origami Solar idea to life, but the newly introduced owner of the tech, Nextpower, is delivering steel frames to the masses. Nextpower, a steel expert through its experience in producing tracking and mounting systems, acquired Origami in 2025 and will use its existing network of steel partners to convince more PV project developers to consider an alternative to aluminum.

It has been revealed that “Nextpower has introduced over 30 manufacturing facilities in the U.S. since 2020. Nextpower buys over 700,000 short tons of primary U.S. steel annually, which is more than a small car firm,” said Jenya Meydbray, VP and general manager of Nextpower’s steel frames business. “Nextpower has had [the steel frame] for one year, building on the years of Origami’s engineering with Welser’s support. What we’re doing today is launching into high-scale, high-volume production here in Ohio.”.

The solar industry defaulted to aluminum panel frames because the material is lightweight, easy to handle and less susceptible to corrosion. But as the solar industry matured, more environmental and practical concerns became associated with the metal. Aluminum production on average has a five-times larger carbon footprint than steel production, a difficult point to ignore in the inherently green solar industry. Solar panels have also gotten larger in surface area and use less glass to cut weight. Aluminum might no longer be the ideal material to physically support these “significant, floppy modules.”.

Industry observers note that A steel coil feeds into a roll-forming machine producing solar panel frames. Credit: Nextpower.

In a recent development, “Steel provides a far better structural support for the [panel] than aluminum does. That was the initial observation that the Origami founders made,” Meydbray said. “They landed on this specific [roll-form] profile. Roll-forming is a precision process. We’re making millions of sticks of solar panel frames a month, and all of them have to be within sub-millimeter of precision across the full length. Welser is 100 years older than America, so Welser is definitely the most experienced in this art form of steel roll-forming.”.

Sources indicate that welser set up North American operations in 2018 after acquiring an automotive roll-form operation in Valley City. The company established a second location in the same industrial park to accommodate its growing client base in the solar, storage and energy industries.

According to recent reports, welser was one of the first roll-form partners to validate Magnelis — a zinc magnesium coating that has “self-healing” properties is capable of lasting 25 years in the field — and found it a great steel coating for solar energy applications. It’s one of the features of NX CoreFrame, Nextpower’s steel solar module frame.

“Coming up with a new coating on steel, you don’t just throw it on the steel and sell it to the market. You have to trial it, validate it, make sure it works,” Johnson said. “Raw zinc — the coating has to be too thick for the longevity that the solar industry needs. Magnelis can go much lighter coating and still produce the same salt spray, same longevity, and it’s cheaper, faster, smarter.”.

Wesler is the latest high-volume production facility for NX CoreFrame, and Nextpower intends to reach 6.5 GW of annual production through additional manufacturing partners across the country.

According to recent reports, with an established steel frame design, the product just needs to find a place on panel manufacturer’s production lines. Origami Solar had been signing supply agreements with U.S. panel assemblers, an activity that has only increased with the Nextpower transition. Meydbray noted the pitch for a domestic supply chain has become more attractive, especially with Nextpower’s established regional steel manufacturing network.

A machine treats steel coil as it travels along a factory line. Credit: Nextpower.

According to recent reports, “Steel strengthens the supply chain of domestic manufacturing facilities. When frames are bought overseas, they spend five, six weeks on the water before they actually arrive to the factory. [Panel companies] have about 2,000 pallets of frames in inventory when they source from overseas,” he mentioned. “We’re able to provide actual just-in-time delivery to our factory clients. We can make deliveries every 48 hours. [They can save room] where they used to have pallets stacked up. There’s also the working capital of having stuff sit on the water for six weeks. Solar panel manufacturing is not a high-margin business, and working capital management is critical.”.

Nextpower has inked supply agreements with many multi-gigawatt panel manufacturers in the United States, including Jinko, T1 and Thornova.

Sources indicate that “This integration of Nextpower steel frames allows us to deliver high-performance modules tailored to the evolving U.S. market,” said Andrea Bodenhagen, global marketing director at Thornova Solar, which is establishing domestic solar cell manufacturing in Oklahoma. “By incorporating U.S.-made steel frames, we strengthen supply chain resilience while helping our customers maximize domestic content and improve project economics.”.

With bonus incentives from the investment tax credit still in play when solar projects use domestic products, an American-made steel frame can make all the difference.

Sources indicate that “When we see projects that have 100% domestic content on the tracker, we know that’s a perfect candidate for steel frames,” Meydbray stated. “Steel frames get 6% domestic content credit. It’s the second cheapest percent after the tracker. A domestically made solar cell is a lot more expensive than an imported solar cell. The frame is the second-most cost-effective way to buy percentage points.”.

According to recent reports, the NX CoreFrame is universal and can be used with any brand’s mounting or tracking system, but there are advantages when the project can be designed more cohesively through one supplier. Nextpower has spent the last year expanding beyond mounting systems, now offering inverter, electrical balance of system and panel products.

Recent findings suggest that “[Nextpower] is ambitious, but it’s not arrogant. It prioritizes the customer relationships it’s built over the years. We spent time with our customers asking where their pain points are and expanded the business accordingly …  the company that makes the thing the solar panel is mounted to is the same company that makes the frame that’s being mounted,” Meydbray said.

Happy Thanksgiving week, folks! You made it to November, which is no small feat in the year of our lord 2026. Despite all those weeks where decades have been happening, you stuck around long enough to see a turkey grace your table once again. Surely you've got a lot to be thankful for, but today we're asking about one specific item on the list: Carmakers. This past year, which automakers have you been thankful for?

This is a pretty broad question, with an appropriately broad criteria set for answers. You don't need to pick a carmaker that introduced a upcoming car you like this past year, or a organization that introduced anything at all since last Thanksgiving — you don't even need to pick a brand that existed in 2026. Instead, all you need is to pick a carmaker that you're glad is or was around, for any reason at all. New cars, new tech, or even just the company that made the used jalopy you just found on Marketplace.

In a recent development, for my part, I'm thankful for Honda. The firm introduced the Prelude late last year, but I didn't start seeing them on my local roads until 2026. Every time I see one of the new Preludes, I'm glad Honda made this little coupe. It may not be particularly sporty, but I like that. If we want automakers to get back into the two-door game, we need to prove that these cars can sell beyond the car enthusiasts of the world, and the Prelude is a great way to make that case.

I'm thankful for Honda this year, but which automaker are you thankful for? Leave your picks down in the comments, and I'll collect my favorites later on in the week. You'll be able to scroll the best-of list on Thanksgiving, in case you need an escape from all those family politics debates. Good luck with those, by the way, and remember that no one can expect an immediate response from you if your mouth is full of mashed potatoes.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith's $42 million Los Angeles property went up in flames after their shed caught fire.
  • The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department and the Malibu/Lost Hills Sheriff’s Station responded to a 911 call at the property in the early hours of Nov.
  • Officials told People that they arrived to discover a "structure fire" at the couple's Calabasas home.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith's $42 million Los Angeles property went up in flames after their shed caught fire.

The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department and the Malibu/Lost Hills Sheriff’s Station responded to a 911 call at the property in the early hours of Nov. 23.

Officials told People that they arrived to discover a "structure fire" at the couple's Calabasas home. They added that no one was hurt.

“It appears a shed caught fire, and the cause is believed to be accidental,” the statement from the sheriff's department revealed.

In audio from the 911 call obtained from Page Six, firefighters can be heard saying, "We do have a shed on fire with no spread to the brush.".

An emergency personnel noted that they were already "on scene," and then another firefighter explained that the fire had been "downgraded to a structure.".

The couple's Calabasas property serves as their primary residence. Set on 150 acres, the estate—which they began working on in 1997, the same year they tied the knot—features high-end amenities, including a basketball court, a tennis court, and a massive swimming pool.

The property was designed by architect Stephen Samuelson, who teamed up with Smith and Pinkett Smith in 1997, after they were inspired by the work he had done on the home of Carol Burnett, according to Architectural Digest.

It has been revealed that however, it was to be a labor of love for the couple—who had to wait four years to secure the permits to begin construction on their dream home. It would sit at the center of an enormous property that they had amassed over time by buying up adjacent plots of land as they became available.

In the end, Smith and Pinkett Smith created an idyllic Mediterranean-inspired sanctuary for their family, boasting all manner of luxury from a meditation lounge and a recording studio to a sunken trampoline.

Recent findings suggest that it was previously believed that Smith and Pinkett Smith were living apart, with the actress revealing during a previous "Today" interview that she had moved into a newly introduced abode in the Los Angeles area. She did not reveal any other details about the property.

The fire comes after Smith, 58, and Pinkett Smith, 55, were spotted in a rare outing alongside their children, Jaden, 28, and Willow, 26.

Last year, the couple put one of their many homes on the market for the relatively low price of $2 million—amid rampant speculation over the state of their marriage.

Many fans have been questioning the status of their relationship since 2022, when Smith infamously slapped Chris Rock across the face during the Oscars ceremony after the comedian made a joke about Pinkett Smith's hair.

Then, just over a year later, Pinkett Smith sensationally revealed during an interview on the "Today" show that she and Smith had been living "completely separate lives" since 2016, despite insisting that they had no plans to legally divorce.

In the two years since that candid confession, questions have continued to be swirl about the truth of their relationship, with Smith sending the rumor mill into overdrive again in February when he put on a very raunchy display with singer India Martínez during an on-stage performance of their song, "First Love.".

Following that public display, the "Men In Black" actor pushed forward a new album, titled "Based on a True Story," marking the first time he has released a new record in years.

According to Smith, the album is the result of "self-examination" that began after the Oscars incident, which saw the actor banned from all academy events for 10 years.

"I’ve taken the last couple of years to really do a deep dive on the parts of me that may or may not been in that level of certainty and asking those deep scary internal questions," he told the Associated Press.

"It really is the result of my initial self-examination. Every song is about some part of myself that I discovered or wanted to explore, something I wanted to share. It’s the most full musical offering that I’ve ever created.".

CrowdStrike’s Zscaler deal is a $44B vote for platformization and a long-term threat to Palo Alto Networks

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2044 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For decades, the security industry has told buyers to choose best-of-breed security products, leaving practitioners to stitch them together.
  • This has been perpetuated by the major analyst firms, which have a Wave for this product and a Magic Quadrant for that product.
  • has long articulated the value of security platformization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:11 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala.

For decades, the security industry has told buyers to choose best-of-breed security products, leaving practitioners to stitch them together.

This has been perpetuated by the major analyst firms, which have a Wave for this product and a Magic Quadrant for that product. The reality is that choosing best-of-breed everywhere has never led to best-in-class threat protection.

Palo Alto Networks Inc. has long articulated the value of security platformization. To be precise, Fortinet Inc. was the first vendor to advance the concept of a security platform, but no security provider has pushed the industry as hard as Palo Alto. Chief Executice Nikesh Arora has been vocal about platforms as the only way to truly protect the entire attack surface.

According to recent reports, crowdStrike Holdings Inc.’s agreement to acquire Zscaler Inc. for $43.9 billion strongly supports the thesis. SiliconANGLE has been covering the deal, so I won’t rehash the details. In short, the leader in endpoint security is buying the leader in cloud-delivered zero-trust access. The combined tech giant is expected to start with more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue, and the deal is expected to close between August 2027 and January 2028.

In a recent development, over the long term, the combination poses a real threat to Palo Alto. In the short term, it is a strong co-sell opportunity for CrowdStrike and Zscaler, with significant integration work between the two.

Arora has long argued that customers want fewer vendors and integrated platforms. Getting there can be challenging, as security teams often operate with an “if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it” mentality. The mere thought of replacing a working product is enough to keep even the most seasoned security pros up at night. In February 2024, when he cut guidance to fund the platform push, Palo Alto’s stock fell 28% in a day. Since then, the stock has recovered nicely, validating his strategy, and its rival has now raised $44 billion to head down its own platform journey.

In some ways, CrowdStrike and Zscaler were the strongest argument against platformization, though one could argue that each was its own smaller “platform,” depending on how you define it. Each led its category, and the two were close partners, with more than 2,000 shared customers and 16 product integrations. If best-of-breed products, tied together by integrations, could work anywhere, it was here. The two companies are now taking it a step further. “When you integrate as partners, there’s only so much you can do,” Zscaler founder and CEO Jay Chaudhry said on the analyst call.

Industry observers note that the “why now?” question is worth asking, as the coming together of these two companies has been rumored for some time. The answer is that agentic AI creates fresh challenges and risks that are difficult to address through a partnership. An AI agent runs on a device and then crosses the network to access models, tools, and data, operating at machine speed around the clock. A vendor that sees only the device or only the network sees only half of what the agent does. CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz mentioned adversaries are “exploiting the seams and the gaps between companies’ integrations.”.

I agree. Every seam between products is a place for an attacker to hide, and AI-driven attacks exploit those seams faster than security teams can close them. But a platform is more than one vendor and one contract. It means one dataset, one agent, and one policy engine, so a detection on a laptop triggers enforcement across the network without a person in the middle. If that’s the standard, CrowdStrike, while it at the moment describes itself as a platform, is not today.

According to recent reports, with Zscaler, CrowdStrike is more than just a product to fill a gap. Zscaler is a best-in-class Secure Access Service Edge stack that protects half of the Fortune 500 and runs what it calls the world’s largest inline security cloud.

It is also built for resilience, which matters more than ever. Last week, I wrote about six major outages over six days at organizations ranging from Microsoft to the Federal Aviation Administration. Zscaler sits between every user and every application, so if it fails, the business stops. That has forced the tech giant to engineer for failure.

Industry observers note that its Business Continuity Cloud provides each customer with a dedicated backup environment in third-party data centers, on separate networks and DNS, with software updates deliberately staggered so a bad release can’t affect both simultaneously. “No linkage — no network, no shared routers, no switches, no shared network operations,” Chaudhry told me in a previous conversation.

Sources indicate that of all companies, CrowdStrike should value that. In July 2024, a faulty Falcon revision affected an estimated 8.5 million Windows devices. The standard objection to platformization is concentration risk, and it intensifies when a single vendor controls both the endpoint agent and the path to every application. Zscaler’s continuity design is the best answer to that objection I’ve seen, and CrowdStrike should extend it across Falcon.

The near-term value is commercial. CrowdStrike says about 8,000 Zscaler customers don’t yet buy from it. Channel partners already sell both companies, and the two sales teams already work deals together.

According to recent reports, after the close, Zscaler will transition to Falcon Flex, CrowdStrike’s licensing model. “A Zscaler customer can add Falcon. A Falcon customer can add Zscaler. One contract, one platform,” Kurtz said. CrowdStrike expects about $1 billion in annualized revenue synergies within 30 months of closing.

This target seems bullish but achievable, as it requires no code integration — only sales execution, which both companies are good at.

Today, the Falcon sensor and Zscaler’s client run as separate agents on separate clouds with different release schedules. Kurtz promised that it will collapse into one. “The brand promise, single agent, that’s not going to change,” he mentioned. CrowdStrike’s next-generation sensor can already inspect and proxy network traffic, he added, which should make the job easier.

In a recent development, kurtz was also candid about the effort: “Yes, there’s hard work to be done. There always is in an acquisition.” CrowdStrike gave no timeline. The engineering teams can’t combine until the deal closes, which is at least eight months away. CrowdStrike’s largest prior acquisition cost less than $1 billion. Folding Zscaler’s global security cloud into Falcon is far harder than anything it has attempted. Until that work is done, the platform exists on slides.

In a recent development, that gap gives Palo Alto time to further its own platform. It closed its CyberArk acquisition in February, renamed the business Idira, and is already cross-selling it to its existing customers.

The long term looks different. If CrowdStrike delivers a single agent and a single dataset, Palo Alto will face something it hasn’t had: a rival of similar scale with the leading endpoint product and the leading zero-trust cloud on one platform. Palo Alto is most exposed in SASE, where its Prisma SASE business has been chasing Zscaler.

Recent findings suggest that crowdStrike plus Zscaler make a formidable platform, but it still lacks a firewall. Zscaler is a cloud proxy, and many enterprises that use it still run firewalls in their data centers, campuses, and clouds. That is Palo Alto’s core area of strength.

Looking ahead, that should open the door to another acquisition. Check Point is the obvious choice, as it will struggle over the long term as a firewall pure-play in a market shifting to platforms, and it would give CrowdStrike a large installed base. If CrowdStrike wants a broader networking portfolio, Fortinet is the bigger swing, with switching, wireless and software-defined wide-area network alongside its firewalls. The two already partner on endpoint and firewall protection.

According to recent reports, either deal would add more integration work to Zscaler, so I wouldn’t expect either to happen soon. But a company that wants to displace Palo Alto can’t leave the firewall to someone else forever. I understand zero trust can replace a number of firewalls, particularly in branch offices, but firewalls are here to stay for the foreseeable future.

The deal also puts smaller security vendors in play. Netskope and Cato Networks are both independent SASE vendors competing against a bundle, and Oppenheimer has already named Netskope an attractive target.

In a recent development, fortinet is an obvious acquirer, but the buyer pool extends beyond security companies. Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co., following its acquisition of Juniper Networks Inc., is embedding security across its network and may seek to bolster that portfolio. Dell Technologies Inc. lags in security, with a portfolio centered on data protection and resilience, and could benefit from an acquisition to close the gap.

Nothing changes today, and customers shouldn’t pause their projects. I’d use the waiting period to prepare in advance.

In a recent development, buy what is integrated. Ask for the integration roadmap with dates for the single agent, the shared data set and unified policy. Until those ship, evaluate CrowdStrike and Zscaler as two products.

Use leverage. Palo Alto is trying to pry Zscaler accounts loose, and CrowdStrike and Zscaler want commitments before the close. As Sanchit Vir Gogia of Greyhound Research told CSO, “Consolidation is sold at the first signature and priced at the second.” Negotiate price caps for renewals now.

Get interoperability in writing. When asked about lock-in, Kurtz stated, “We have and will continue to work well with all of the other technologies and ecosystem.” If you run Zscaler with another endpoint product or Falcon with another access provider, include that promise in your contract.

According to recent reports, make resilience a requirement. Ask CrowdStrike to commit to maintaining Zscaler’s Business Continuity Cloud and its staggered updates, and to apply the same discipline to a combined agent.

In a recent development, this deal settles the argument over platformization. Who wins is still unclear. CrowdStrike has to do the integration work, and Palo Alto has the better part of a year to persuade customers not to wait. The great news for customers is that big moves like this create a wave of innovation. AI is changing security faster than ever before, and a CrowdStrike-vs.-Palo Alto battle is good for everyone.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) is an interesting piece of legislation. It is getting a ton of support from the solar sector, but it is heavily opposed by environmental organizations.

Recent findings suggest that following the passage of BAAJA in the US Senate the other day, Tim Pawlenty, CEO of the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA), stated the following: “America is now one step closer to lower energy costs, more clean energy and a more reliable electric grid. Senators Lee, Capito, Heinrich, and Whitehouse deserve tremendous credit for advancing this bipartisan bill.”.

Sources indicate that the organization adds some more detail and why it thinks this is such a good piece of legislation: “SEIA analysis reveals that BAAJA could unlock 167 gigawatts of additional solar capacity between 2028 and 2035, bringing solar to over 18% of U.S. electricity generation by 2035. The analysis finds that the bill’s reforms could reduce cumulative power sector CO2 emissions by approximately 20% and avoid $54 billion in public health damages.”.

It has been revealed that that sounds very appealing, doesn’t it? Why wouldn’t we want that?

Recent findings suggest that well, the Sierra Club argues the bill goes in quite the opposite direction. The storied organization states the following: “While a rogue president is waging a war on clean energy, the Senate rushed a deeply flawed bill that furthers the buildout of fossil fuels, strips away power from communities and Tribes, threatens our clean water and public lands, and endangers wildlife. The House of Representatives has an equal voice in the legislative process. They must reject the Senate’s fast-tracked bill and demand debate and consideration to deliver for the people, not corporate polluters and Donald Trump. The American people made a clear call merely weeks ago: our elected leaders must address soaring costs and a corrupt system that prioritizes corporate polluter profits over our health, our wallets, and our future.”.

It seems the glitch is that BAAJA would make it much easier to put up power plants, skipping all kinds of environmental protections. That is why Republicans support it in the first place — they are always keen to plow through environmental protections. The reason SEIA supports it is clear enough — the organization is just thinking about solar power plants and looking at the potential for more growth in the industry, especially considering the fact that solar is now typically the cheapest option for fresh power capacity and has been dominating new installations.

So, the question is: would BAAJA really disproportionately support solar power, or would it lead to a lot more fossil fuel power plants and an edge to the old, dirty power technologies? Can the legislation be both good and bad, or is someone getting this wrong?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Happy Tuesday! It's November 24, 2026, and this is The Morning Shift — your daily roundup of the top automotive headlines from around the world, in one place. This is where you'll find the most important stories that are shaping the way Americans drive and get around.

In this morning's edition we're looking at the Department of Defense getting GM and Ford into the drone business, and Tesla pushing its driver assistance on the elderly. We'll also look at Volkswagen's battle against its workers, and Ineos moving stateside.

Under the Trump administration, the United States government has shifted from a focus on soft power — international aid, alliances, things of that nature — to focusing entirely on hard military power. Gone are the days of USAID, now is the era of massing drones. Only, there's a problem: U.S. drone makers can't actually make enough to keep up with Department of Defense orders. Thus, a new push from the Pentagon, to get automakers into the drone business. From the Wall Street Journal:.

The Pentagon is in talks with General Motors and other manufacturers to help mass produce drones, according to people familiar with the matter, the latest effort by the U.S. military to enlist the car industry's sprawling assembly lines to increase production of critical munitions and equipment.

Under a deal, auto companies would supply parts to drone companies, the people mentioned. Among the scenarios: GM is weighing whether to manufacture drone motors, albeit closer in size to something that would power a riding lawn mower than a car. Defense officials have met with leaders at Ford Motor, Canadian parts giant Magna International and other manufacturing companies, including outside the auto industry.

Responses from automakers around drone building have been "mixed," according to the WSJ, but we live in an era where the President can hand-pick who runs companies in spite of all manner of allegations. Do we really think any U.S.-based firm in its right mind would say no to such a man? Maybe an automaker could stall until the latest legislative session in January, but that doesn't remove Trump from power.

Tesla doesn't so much care about selling its cars as it does selling its software these days, and the company seems to have its sights set on a new frontier of driver-assistance software: The elderly. If you're wondering what happens when you combine technology that lulls drivers into a false sense of security with drivers whose reflexes and powers of perception are failing them, well, we're about to find out. From Bloomberg:.

Sources indicate that tesla warns consumers that FSD requires drivers to pay attention and be prepared to take immediate action at all times. It acknowledges none of its driver-assistance features make Teslas autonomous. And yet the firm is increasingly promoting the merits of the system to seniors, further muddling the already complex question of when the moment has come for older drivers to give up their car keys.

It has been revealed that experts say the technology's limitations may actually raise risks for the elderly. The pitfalls of aging, including changes in vision, loss of physical mobility and slower reflexes, can impair an older driver's ability to safely take control when needed.

It has been revealed that the core issue here is a thorny one. On the one hand, seniors still need to get around — grocery delivery isn't always an option on a fixed income, and socializing staves off dementia. On the other hand, people whose faculties are decaying probably shouldn't be controlling thousands of pounds of metal that hurtle through our roads, especially with software that only demands occasional-yet-immediate engagement rather than constant attention. The answer is buses, but no one wants to talk about that.

Volkswagen, one of the world's largest carmakers, thinks it's too big. To compete with lower-cost competitors from China, the firm is trying to scale back its own costs — by cutting production and people. Those people are, understandably, not super psyched about these decisions. From Reuters:.

EMDEN, Germany, Nov 24 (Reuters) – Volkswagen began crunch ‌wage talks with labour representatives on Tuesday amid mounting worker anger over deep cost cuts, with protesters carrying black coffins to symbolise what they remarked was the death of trust and the tech giant's future prospects.

The first round of talks takes place in the northern German ​town of Emden, home to one of the factories fighting for survival, where around 4,000 workers protested before representatives of the IG Metall ​union ad the automaker's works council met Volkswagen management.

"If necessary, there will also be industrial action of a kind never before seen at Volkswagen," works council head Daniela Cavallo told workers chanting "strike-ready" and carrying black coffins inscribed with the words "future" and "trust".

It has been revealed that when your workers start carrying coffins around to show the long-term costs of your short-sighted decision making, it's probably worth listening to them. Volkswagen's idea to cut its staff and production capacity to the bone is the sort of move that works on a spreadsheet, but realistically hampers the firm's ability to be agile in a market that's seen constant changes from shifting international regulations and upcoming competitors. Essentially, the company is looking to specialize in doing things in a way that works right now, with the hope that the current circumstances never change.

Recent findings suggest that ineos, a company I occasionally remember exists and is real, wants to sell in the U.S. without tariffs. To do so, it's looking to start production on our shores, and it's going to make the numbers work by getting rid of one of its European factories — specifically, by selling a French factory to BYD. From Automotive News:.

Ineos Automotive, hampered by President Donald Trump's import tariffs, is ready to build in the U.S.

In a recent development, the small British automaker mentioned it has identified a short list of U.S. sites where it plans to produce pickups and SUVs. At the same time the organization, in a major pivot, plans to sell its French assembly plant to Chinese automaker BYD.

The two moves would have major repercussions on both sides of the Atlantic Ocean: Ineos would gain a manufacturing footprint in the country where it generates 70 percent of its global sales, and BYD would collect another European plant.

This is the kind of knock-on effect that's hard to predict when you institute tariffs. Sure, production of the Ineos Grenadier expands into the U.S., and that plays well with the UAW folks from whom Trump wants votes, it also enables a further BYD foothold in Europe, though, emboldening a Chinese competitor that Trump would rather see quashed.

The LiTime Lares K1 Expandable Plug & Play Kitchen Backup — CleanTechnica Tested

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1246 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, I spent 35 years in the Tampa suburbs, so I pay attention to backup power when a storm  is coming.
  • It has been revealed that liTime launched the Lares K1 in the US on October 20, 2026.
  • The inverter puts out 2,000 watts continuously and 4,000 watts of surge power for one second, as a pure sine wave at 120 volts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I spent 35 years in the Tampa suburbs, so I pay attention to backup power when a storm  is coming. Last year I tested the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 portable power station for CleanTechnica. That unit is meant to be carried around. The LiTime Lares K1 is different: a plug-in kitchen backup battery you leave in place and hook up to a refrigerator and also use to power your small kitchen appliances. First I’ll go through the specs and how it compares with a portable station like the Elite 100 V2, then I’ll give my test results.

It has been revealed that liTime launched the Lares K1 in the US on October 20, 2026. It is a split system: a slim inverter charger paired with a separate 2,304 watt-hour LiFePO4 battery (51.2 volts, 45 amp-hours). You can add up to four batteries, which brings the total to 9,216 watt-hours. The battery is rated for 4,000 cycles, and LiTime backs it with a 5-year warranty.

The inverter puts out 2,000 watts continuously and 4,000 watts of surge power for one second, as a pure sine wave at 120 volts. Adding batteries does not raise that output. You just get more runtime. There are two AC outlets, one on each side of the inverter. I did not see any USB ports listed.

Industry observers note that you can charge it at up to 1,500 watts from a wall outlet and up to 800 watts from solar (12 to 60 volts). Combined input is capped at 1,500 watts. LiTime does not put a charge time on the main product page. If you divide 2,304 watt-hours by the 1,500-watt wall input, you get about 90 minutes from empty to full. That is a rough estimate. Charging usually slows down as you get close to 100%, the same way an EV does, and their FAQ later puts the theoretical time at about 1.7 hours if you figure 90% charging efficiency.

It has been revealed that the inverter charger weighs about 10.1 pounds. LiTime does not list the battery weight, but I weighted it after I took it out of the packaging and it was about 52 pounds. With the floor stand, the two modules stood up together are 20.47 inches wide, 30.71 inches tall, and 3.94 inches deep. It runs at about 40 decibels (which is very quiet) and switches over to battery in 10 milliseconds or less. It has a touchscreen, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth 5.0, and the LiTime app, plus a time-of-use mode so you can charge off-peak.

In a recent development, the price on LiTime’s site is $1,099.99, shown as $100 off. US preorders opened October 20, 2026, and when I checked, estimated delivery was November 24 to 27.

It has been revealed that liTime calls this “space-based” home backup. Instead of trying to power the whole house, you protect one room, in this case the kitchen. You plug the system into a wall outlet and plug the fridge into the K1. No electrician and no panel work. LiTime estimates about 24 hours of backup on a large side-by-side refrigerator (while I got a bit more than that in my testing) that uses about 2 kilowatt-hours a day, or about 99 hours with four batteries if the fridge is the only load. Depending on the load, it can also run a microwave, an air fryer, a toaster, or a coffee maker for a basic meal. Just don’t try to run them all at once. You can run two smaller loads at once, but a large load like a microwave or air fryer needs to be run by itself (you can keep your refrigerator plugged in too). LiTime notes to allow for compressor startup if you also want to run one of those at the same time.

Sources indicate that you can wall-mount it, stand it on the floor, or lean it against a wall, with the two modules together or apart. It comes with mounting hardware and two connection cables, 0.25 meters and 1.5 meters (about 10 inches and 5 feet). The battery housing is steel, and LiTime indicates the metal finish is meant to suit a kitchen. The inverter is rated IP20, so it stays indoors. LiTime says separating the inverter from the battery cuts down on heat transfer, which they claim helps the battery last longer. I have not measured that.

Sources indicate that for a plug & play system, this is a new product category. There have been portable generators available for years that could be used for camping or appliance backup, but having a product tailored to a specific room is a new concept. The comparison they offer is this one-room approach versus a whole-house battery system, the kind that usually needs panel work and that will cost you about 10 times as much.

You can use this for camping or travel, but it isn’t built for it. With split modules, wall-mount hardware, only two AC outlets, and no USB ports, this is built for a permanent kitchen install, not something you toss in the car for a weekend trip.

I used my old Kill-A-Watt meter to have an independent measure of the draw on the battery from the refrigerator. During the test, I opened the refrigerator less than I normally would, but still opened it about 10 times.

Next I wanted to test it with my small kitchen appliances. First, one at a time; then, several at once. It is rated at 2000 watts continuous, but it should be able to surge up to 4000 watts for 1 second.

Industry observers note that notice that it pulls 2510 watts from the battery, but the load is only 2290 watts. Where did the other 220 watts go? That must be used by the inverter to convert DC to AC.

After 35 years of Tampa storm seasons, I’ve learned that the fridge is usually the first thing you worry about when the power goes out. The LiTime Lares K1 is built for exactly that. In my testing it kept our large side-by-side GE refrigerator running for almost 26 hours on one battery, a bit longer than LiTime’s own estimate of 24 hours. It then shut off cleanly to protect the appliance. Recharging from the wall took about 3 hours, with 80% back in about 2 hours.

It also handled my small kitchen appliances well. The air fryer, coffee maker, and refrigerator ran together at about 2,200 watts, a little over the rated 2,000. When I added the toaster to push it past its limits, it briefly put out about 3,140 watts and then dropped back to about 2,130 watts without shutting down. The app also demonstrated about 220 watts lost in converting battery power to AC, which is worth keeping in mind when you estimate runtime.

It does have limits. There are only two outlets, no USB ports, and the battery weighs about 52 pounds, so this is a permanent kitchen install, not a camping generator. Adding batteries gives you more runtime, but not more output.

According to recent reports, at $1,099.99, with no electrician or panel work needed and a 5-year battery warranty, the Lares K1 is an affordable way to protect your food and still cook a basic meal during an outage. It costs about a tenth of what a whole-house battery would. If kitchen backup is what you care about most, it’s well worth a look.

Why an Uninsulated Garage Can Wreak Havoc on Your Home This Winter
