The 9,843-square-foot estate, tucked away on a private peninsula, features a six-bedroom primary residence and a detached guest residence connected by a walking bridge. Designed for grand-scale entertaining, the light-filled open floor strategy includes a stunning two-story great room with floor-to-ceiling windows capturing the oceanfront views; a chef's kitchen with a butler's pantry, catering area, and wine room; and a sun-soaked primary suite with a sitting room, two vanities, dual water closets, a walk-in shower, and a soaking tub.

Garden pathways wind through the lushly landscaped lot, which also has a reflective saltwater pond, a heated swimming pool with a waterfall grotto, a private beach, and multiple waterfront entertainment spaces.

Offering direct access to the Atlantic Ocean, the property has approximately 450 feet of dockage extending into a protected basin, along with an air-conditioned boathouse, a tackle room, and a workshop.

Eric Rizzo of Ocean Sotheby's International Realty is the listing agent.

The Atlantic Anchor: This seven-bedroom coastal retreat is remarked to be owned by real estate developer Daniel E. Edwards, who purchased the 1.02-acre property for $22 million in 2023.

Built in 2020 in the private enclave of Harbor Court, which comprises just two oceanfront estates, this 15,150-square-foot mansion has 150 feet of frontage along the Atlantic Ocean. The elegant interior features an elevator, a private office, a third-floor clubroom with a bar and home theater, a 500-bottle wine cellar, and a primary suite with dual spa-inspired bathrooms and a wraparound terrace with Atlantic-facing views. Covered patios overlook the resort-inspired free-form pool with waterfalls, a waterslide, and a spa.

A tennis court, a temperature-controlled garage with RV-height doors, a workshop, a professional-grade golf simulator, and a two-bedroom guesthouse with an elevator are also on the property.

The Matt and Nick Team of Serhant is the listing agent.

According to The Real Deal, a liquidation entity for Shapiro's Woodbridge Group of Companies sold the 20,541-square-foot mansion for $35 million in 2019 to the current owner.

The show kitchen has dual marble islands, a wine cellar, and a secondary catering kitchen. The primary suite has a leather wall, a private lounge, a soaking tub, and dual closets. The primary wing has book-matched Golden onyx, a spa bath, a plunge pool, and a cantilevered cliffside office. A commercial kitchen was designed for entertaining. The home is being offered fully furnished.

A $1,812 monthly association fee provides access to championship golf, a 13,000-square-foot wellness center, and fine dining.

Ginger Glass of Compass is the listing agent.

Palazzo Della Luna: This full-floor penthouse owned by Kayak CEO Steve Hafner last changed hands for $40 million in 2021.

Spanning the entire 10th floor, the five-bedroom condo was designed to feature breathtaking views from nearly every room. Built in 2019, the 10,194-square-foot open floor blueprint features 15-foot ceilings and floor-to-ceiling glass walls that capture vistas stretching from the Atlantic Ocean and Biscayne Bay to Government Cut, Fisher Island, and the Miami skyline.

It also has a private 7,322-square-foot rooftop terrace, along with nearly 2,000 square feet of covered wraparound terraces to soak in the ocean and city scenery.

Jill Eber of Coldwell Banker Realty is the listing agent.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
CMS issues Medicare Advantage proposals aimed at boosting competition" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration has proposed a slew of changes to Medicare Advantage and Part D designed to "revitalize care" in these markets.

For one, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said late Friday that it will upgrade application and network adequacy requirements to make it easier for latest entrants. The agency proposed to require organizations to demonstrate network adequacy during their first year in operation, rather than during the application process.

This shift would eliminate a significant barrier for new entrants, driving greater competition in the market.

CMS has also proposed combining three specialty areas in behavioral health—clinical psychology, clinical social work and outpatient behavioral health—into one specialty group for the purposes of network adequacy. The changes will give plans greater flexibility in building out behavioral health networks.

CMS will also make adjustments that seek to boost competition for special needs plans.

In addition, the agency said it will make adjustments to the star ratings program, focusing its ratings on 15 measures. The proposed measure set would emphasize "clinical outcomes and patient experience while retaining select process measures in high-priority areas where performance remains low.".

CMS is also aiming to patch the calculation methodology that will "raise the bar for achieving high ratings," and thus quality bonus payments.

Recent findings suggest that "People with Medicare should be able to choose coverage based on what matters most to them—quality, affordability and access," said CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., in the announcement. "These proposals are about creating a Medicare Advantage marketplace that rewards better care and better value while empowering beneficiaries with the options and knowledge they need to make informed decisions about their health.".

In a recent development, the proposed rule also includes provisions that align with Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy's Make America Healthy Again agenda by setting a "healthy food" standard that MA plans should follow for supplemental benefits.

The goal, CMS mentioned, is to ensure that Medicare dollars are spent on food benefits that align with MAHA.

"Medicare food benefits should pay for nutritious food that helps people improve their health and manage chronic disease," Kennedy stated in the announcement. "This proposal would require those benefits to meet the Dietary Guidelines for Americans while preserving access to foods and nutritional products that providers recommend for patients’ specific medical needs.".

"Under President Trump, we are putting prevention at the center of health care and demanding more from every Medicare dollar," Kennedy said.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A growing body of research suggests that aging may be more flexible than once believed.
  • Recent findings suggest that their findings suggest that certain prescription medications and lifestyle changes can reduce biological age as measured by DNA-based blood tests.
  • The findings, published in Nature Medicine, could help scientists evaluate anti-aging treatments more effectively, although researchers emphasize that changes in biological age markers do not necessarily mean people will live longer or avoid age-related diseases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A growing body of research suggests that aging may be more flexible than once believed. Now, scientists at Yale have taken an vital step toward identifying which treatments can actually influence biological aging and which ones show little measurable benefit.

Recent findings suggest that their findings suggest that certain prescription medications and lifestyle changes can reduce biological age as measured by DNA-based blood tests. Popular over-the-counter supplements examined in the research, however, demonstrated little evidence of producing the same effects.

The findings, published in Nature Medicine, could help scientists evaluate anti-aging treatments more effectively, although researchers emphasize that changes in biological age markers do not necessarily mean people will live longer or avoid age-related diseases.

From Fighting Cancer to Understanding Aging.

When Raghav Sehgal began graduate school at Yale several years ago, he planned to use advanced computer science techniques to investigate cancer. His background in engineering and experience launching a computational biology startup had given him a strong foundation for that work.

It has been revealed that however, a question from his Ph.D. adviser at the Yale School of Medicine changed his research direction. Rather than focusing on individual diseases such as cancer or cardiovascular disease, why not investigate the aging process that contributes to their development?

"That put me on a different path," noted Sehgal, now an associate research scientist in psychiatry who specializes in computational biology and bioinformatics. "As researchers, we have a long way to go in understanding the aging process and whether the steps we take to manage it really work.".

In a recent development, sehgal now studies the biological mechanisms behind human aging, how scientists can measure those changes, and why getting older increases the likelihood of conditions such as cancer, diabetes, and dementia. His work also explores whether interventions might reverse certain aspects of biological aging, even if eliminating aging itself remains beyond reach.

New DNA Tests Reveal Which Anti-Aging Treatments Work.

Sehgal is the lead author of the upcoming study, which was conducted in the laboratory of Albert Higgins-Chen, an assistant professor of psychiatry at the Yale School of Medicine. The research team set out to determine which existing approaches to slowing aging produce changes that can be reliably measured.

Their analysis found encouraging results for certain medications and lifestyle interventions. In contrast, the over-the-counter supplements included in the study generally failed to produce meaningful reductions in biological age.

In a recent development, the project involved the entire Higgins-Chen laboratory, including Daniel Borrus, Jenel F. Armstrong, John Gonzalez, Jessica Kasamoto, and Yaroslav Markov.

According to recent reports, "For the first time we've shown that certain therapies have measurable impacts," said Sehgal. "This wasn't previously possible, because we didn't have enough data to say these biomarkers are consistently responsive to these interventions.".

It has been revealed that biomarkers provide measurable information about what is happening inside the body. In aging research, they can help estimate a person's biological or functional age, which may differ from their chronological age.

How Scientists Measure Biological Age.

To investigate whether treatments could influence aging, the Yale team relied primarily on blood-based measurements called epigenetic clocks.

These tools analyze chemical patterns attached to DNA, particularly methyl groups (basic chemical structures that act like tags). Previous research has shown that these chemical markers change as people grow older. Some interventions may reverse certain age-associated patterns, and computer algorithms use those changes to estimate a person's biological age.

The researchers brought together findings from 51 clinical studies investigating different anti-aging strategies. These ranged from dietary supplements and medications to lifestyle changes and medical procedures.

According to recent reports, across those studies, the team examined more than 110 DNA methylation biomarkers (including 16 major epigenetic clocks). By comparing measurements taken before and after interventions, they could evaluate which approaches were associated with reductions in biological age.

"What we did was pretty unique," Sehgal noted. "We already know that certain things might prolong health span and lifespan. There is data from retrospective analysis as well as from animal models. We took all that knowledge along with the real-world clinical studies to identify which interventions in humans were slowing down aging across the board in these known biomarkers.".

Which Anti-Aging Treatments Showed the Best Results?

The researchers divided the interventions into four main groups: prescription drugs, lifestyle modifications, over-the-counter supplements, and medical procedures.

One of the clearest findings involved diet and exercise. Combining regular physical activity with a healthy eating plan consistently reduced epigenetic age. The dietary approaches examined included Mediterranean, low-fat, and low-carb diets.

Recent findings suggest that the strongest reductions in biological age markers were associated with certain pharmaceutical treatments. These included metformin and semaglutide, prescription medications used to manage metabolic conditions and body weight, as well as anti-TNF therapies that target a protein involved in the body's inflammatory response.

(TNF, or tumor necrosis factor, is an immune-system protein that helps fight inflammation-related injury.).

The findings were less encouraging for over-the-counter supplements and some medical procedures. In the studies examined, these approaches did not produce measurable reductions in epigenetic age.

The researchers also discovered that newer biological age clocks performed better than older versions. Another crucial finding was that people living with diseases generally experienced larger changes in their aging biomarkers than healthy participants.

Could DNA Blood Tests Transform Anti-Aging Research?

Industry observers note that according to Sehgal, the next priority is to test these findings in larger, more diverse populations. This would help researchers determine how consistently different treatments influence biological aging across people with different health conditions and backgrounds.

The improved blood tests could also dramatically shorten the time needed to evaluate potential anti-aging therapies.

In a recent development, "If these newly introduced biomarkers are eventually validated to predict long-term health, scientists will be able to evaluate anti-aging therapies much faster," he added. "Instead of waiting decades for evidence from clinical trials, we'll be able to see which interventions are effective and in which people in a few years or even months.".

In a recent development, that possibility could represent a major advance for aging research. Instead of relying entirely on clinical studies that follow participants for decades, scientists might eventually use validated biological age measurements to identify promising treatments much earlier.

However, senior author Higgins-Chen stressed that scientists must be careful about interpreting what changes in aging biomarkers actually mean.

Sources indicate that "We have developed a rigorous, systematic approach to evaluating and comparing how biomarkers change across a wide variety of interventions, and that is a critical step in the right direction," he stated. "However, the true meaning of that change must be fully understood.".

Key Questions About Slowing Aging Remain.

Although the results are promising, several major questions remain unanswered.

For example, researchers still need to establish whether changes in biological age are directly caused by a treatment or influenced by other factors that were not accounted for. They also need to understand how rapidly those changes occur, whether they persist after treatment ends, and which biological processes produce them.

Most importantly, scientists have not yet established whether lowering epigenetic age leads to meaningful improvements in long-term health.

"And most importantly - what does the change mean for our long-term risk of age-related disease and functional decline?" Higgins-Chen said.

Further investigations into these questions are underway, with additional studies led by Borrus, Armstrong, and Grace Zou.

The Higgins-Chen laboratory is also affiliated with Yale's Department of Pathology, the Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Program, and the Y-Age Yale Center for Research on Aging.

What Appears to Work Against Biological Aging?

Based on the improved DNA-based blood tests, the Yale researchers identified two particularly promising approaches for reducing biological age markers:.

The analysis also identified benefits from certain anti-TNF medications, while the tested over-the-counter supplements and some medical procedures demonstrated little measurable effect.

Sources indicate that these results provide a clearer picture of which interventions may influence biological aging. However, more research is needed to confirm the findings and determine whether reductions in biological age markers ultimately translate into fewer age-related diseases, better health, or longer lives.

Inside a Initiative To Convert Shipping Containers From the Border Wall Into Affordable Housing

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1095 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Flying over the Arizona desert one day in 2023, Beau Phillips looked out his plane window and spotted thousands of shipping containers—remnants of a dismantled border wall—scattered across the arid landscape.
  • That chance glimpse sparked an idea: convert the abandoned steel boxes into hundreds of affordable housing units and build a whole new community in the Tucson area for some of the 40,000 low-income residents waiting for housing assistance.
  • "These were built to keep people out, and now we're welcoming people in," Phillips tells Realtor.com®.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Flying over the Arizona desert one day in 2023, Beau Phillips looked out his plane window and spotted thousands of shipping containers—remnants of a dismantled border wall—scattered across the arid landscape.

That chance glimpse sparked an idea: convert the abandoned steel boxes into hundreds of affordable housing units and build a whole new community in the Tucson area for some of the 40,000 low-income residents waiting for housing assistance.

"These were built to keep people out, and now we're welcoming people in," Phillips tells Realtor.com®. "There is a poetic justice there.".

Phillips, a semiretired MTV Networks and radio marketing executive, first encountered the containers in late 2022, when he took part in a demonstration protesting then-Arizona Gov. Doug Ducey's order to install a border barrier made up of more than 2,000 double-stacked steel shipping crates, topped with wire, near Yuma and in the Coronado National Forest.

After the Biden administration and environmental groups successfully sued, arguing that the 10-mile wall of containers was illegally placed on federal and tribal land, the state took the barrier apart in early 2023.

Some 2,200 steel boxes were left in the desert with no blueprint for their disposal, until Phillips saw them from a plane and pitched state officials on a new use for them.

To bring his vision to life, Phillips founded a nonprofit, Boxes of Hope, and teamed up with La Frontera AZ, a major affordable housing developer and behavioral health provider, to create a village made up of 350 to 450 shipping containers transformed into rental homes.

This project is aimed at singles, couples, veterans, seniors, and anyone priced out of Tucson’s rental market, where the median asking rent in October was $1,133, according to the latest data from Realtor.com.

"We're really opening it up wide to just whoever needs it, and we will make sure that the rent that is charged is affordable," notes Phillips.

Sources indicate that the proposed 25- to 30-acre community will take shape in Southeast Tucson, within 2 miles of the containers' current resting place to minimize transport costs. The site also sits along a bus line and within a half-mile of shopping.

Phillips, who freely admits that he knows "nothing about swinging a hammer," tapped Tucson native Ryan Egan, a veteran container-conversion expert, to lead construction on the ambitious building project, which is presently in the fundraising stage.

It takes about $59,000 to turn a 4-ton crate into a comfortable 300-square-foot residence insulated against Arizona's brutal 115-degree summers.

"It's about half the price that the city of Tucson now pays for-profit builders to build affordable housing, so they're thrilled," notes Phillips.

Each unit will be air-conditioned, with a private bedroom and queen bed, full bathroom, kitchenette with a refrigerator and a two-burner stovetop, storage, latest flooring, windows, and sliding glass doors.

"It would be almost like someone who lives in an RV park," explains the Boxes of Hope founder and CEO. "You have your unit that you live in, and you connect to utilities on site.".

The exteriors will be sandblasted and decorated with colorful murals celebrating Tucson's culture.

Beyond providing a roof and four walls, Phillips and his project partner, La Frontera CEO Dan Ranieri, envision a holistic neighborhood complete with a park, laundry facilities, a community kitchen and dining hall, behavioral healthcare, transitional housing for the homeless, and on-site training in building trades like carpentry and plumbing,.

"It's really a 360-degree solution to get people not just a place to live, but a place where they can thrive," says Phillips.

Sources indicate that boxes of Hope already has backing from Sen. Mark Kelly's office, the Arizona Department of Housing, and Tucson city leadership. The nonprofit is currently meeting with potential donors and pursuing government and private housing grants to move the project from planning into construction.

To any locals harboring "not in my backyard" concerns about the future affordable rental community, Phillips stresses that his team aims to be good neighbors from the start.

"We're going to meet with neighborhood groups. We're going to explain our vision," he notes. " We want to listen to people, but we also want them to understand that we're trying to do something good here. We're trying to take lemons and turn them into lemonade.".

He points to La Frontera's track record of managing affordable housing, which includes the development of nearly a dozen low-income tax credit projects since 2008.

Boxes of Hope plans to unveil its full development initiative and the village's exact location site in January 2027, after signing a letter of intent with the landowner.

"He loves the concept so much that he dropped his price in half and said, 'I want to help you,'" Phillips recalls.

It has been revealed that despite the project's ambitious scope, the construction timeline moves quickly. Turning a raw container into a finished home takes about two weeks, and once production ramps up, Phillips expects the team to complete 12 to 15 conversions per month.

Site development is set to get underway in spring 2027, with the first tenants poised to move in by the second half of next year.

Beyond Tucson, Phillips believes that Boxes of Hope could serve as a blueprint for tackling America's broader housing affordability crisis.

According to recent reports, " Last year, 25 million shipping containers arrived in the U.S. along the West Coast and never left because America doesn't export anywhere near as much as we import," he indicates. "Most of them are still sitting all along the West Coast in Seattle and San Diego and San Francisco and Portland.".

That need for well-priced rental inventory is felt acutely nationwide. According to the latest Realtor.com monthly rental report, the median asking rent in October rose year over year for the first time since 2023, driven by a sharp decline in multifamily construction,.

However, Realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu points out that container conversions have inherent limitations.

"A container can be converted into a studio fairly easily, but it is hard to build larger units with multiple bedrooms that meet the needs of families," she states.

Photon pharmacy marketplace integrated with ChatGPT for clinicians" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Photon, a prescription infrastructure tech giant, is now available as a plugin for ChatGPT to streamline prescribing for clinicians within a tool they already use.

It has been revealed that the option is available to eligible U.S. licensed clinicians using ChatGPT for Clinicians (free for verified clinicians) or ChatGPT for Healthcare. Just as clinicians must accept OpenAI’s BAA before sharing protected patient information, they must accept Photon’s BAA to maintain HIPAA compliance when using Photon in ChatGPT. Controlled substances are not supported. The feature is free for clinicians through Dec. 31, 2026.

The patient experience remains the same through Photon. What is latest is where the clinician can write a prescription. Clinicians with a Photon account can draft, review and send prescriptions without leaving ChatGPT. They just need to add the Photon plugin into ChatGPT, and then they can draft prescriptions. A patient will get a text to Photon’s prescription marketplace outside of ChatGPT. Patients can compare prices and request to change a pharmacy as needed.

Sources indicate that “AI is moving from note-taking and reference into treatment workflows. Clinicians are already using ChatGPT to understand treatment options. Once they’ve decided what to prescribe, they should be able to act on that decision in the same conversation,” Otto Sipe, co-founder and CEO, wrote to Fierce Healthcare in an emailed comment. “Photon provides the infrastructure behind that step.”.

Industry observers note that in the latest interface, clinicians begin a prompt with the name of the patient and medication. Photon uses authorized patient information and treatment context shared with ChatGPT to help prepare a prescription for a clinician’s review. They can also add new patient details during the process. Once saved in Photon, that patient can be found by name for future prescriptions.

From there, clinicians review the prescribing details, including the dosing, instructions and quantity. Clinicians can ask about dosing options in the chat. Patient records are saved in Photon, and draft prescriptions are checked against the patient’s recorded allergies and medications. Finally, clinicians review and authorize the prescription to be sent, remaining responsible for the treatment. Clinicians can check a prescription’s status in ChatGPT.

#99324. AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1702 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, more than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year.
  • Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.
  • The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, more than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.

Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.

The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.

The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.

AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss.

The results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.

According to recent reports, using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.

Importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.

Another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely upcoming type of medical test.

The findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.

"Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," said Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops.".

Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict.

In a recent development, sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.

Recent findings suggest that immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially crucial.

For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.

Because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.

It has been revealed that "One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer stated. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late.".

The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening.

Recent findings suggest that doctors currently rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.

In a recent development, but obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.

Sources indicate that the approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.

At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.

"In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer noted. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things.".

The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.

How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns.

Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.

The researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.

Industry observers note that the AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.

This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.

In a recent development, "Good AI starts with good data," noted Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a big part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today.".

Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.

According to recent reports, "It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer mentioned. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a significant return when they get over the finish line.".

From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments.

The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.

Obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.

Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.

Industry observers note that these longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.

For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.

Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.

Could AI Reveal New Secrets About the Human Heart?

Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.

Rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to latest insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.

Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most notable contributions to medicine, opening upcoming directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.

"There is also going to be a fresh way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer said, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening.".

Sources indicate that fierce Healthcare is tracking workforce changes across healthcare in 2026. Stick with this tracker for the latest updates, and reach out to the team with any layoff news. Also, take a look back at our trackers for 2025 and 2024.

RWJBarnabas Health disclosed intends to eliminate 106 jobs in a New Jersey Department of Labor & Workforce Development filing.

According to recent reports, the notice lists Feb. 16 and Feb. 17 as the effective dates of the cuts, which will occur among roles based in West Orange, New Jersey.

The cuts reflect about 0.3% of the 47,000-person system's total workforce, and are a response to "ongoing funding and regulatory pressures" that have forced the organization to reevaluate its long-term operations, RWJBarnabas Health noted in a statement given to press.

"This includes identifying efficiencies across the organization to ensure affordability and allocating resources where needed to remain strong, resilient and well-positioned for the future,” the statement reads.

Industry observers note that the system said that it is providing support to those affected, including by allowing them to apply to other open positions in the organization. It did not specify the types of roles being affected.

Electronic health record and software manufacturer athenahealth is laying off about 4% of its total workforce, according to a Boston Globe report and subsequent LinkedIn posts from affected workers.

Sources indicate that CEO Bob Segert reportedly informed employees in a Nov. 13 email, in which he cited healthcare provider visits "below our expectations," an overly complex organizational structure and opportunities for AI to "rethink the work itself," according to the Globe.

According to recent reports, the manufacturer has not given a hard number on how many employees are affected. Its last round of layoffs in early 2023 trimmed 178 jobs, which at the time reflected less than 3% of its total workforce.

Ascension will begin laying off 51 St. Louis workers on Jan. 8, according to a Nov. 6 WARN notice filed with the Missouri Office of Workforce Development.

The cuts are reportedly tied to the health system's decision to hand the administration of its employee health plan to Luminare Health, a Health Care Service Corp. subsidiary. That change takes effect Jan. 1, with the health plan for Ascension employees and their dependents changing its branding from SmartHealth to the Ascension Health Plan.

A representative of the health system told press the partners are working to offer potential retention or placement support ahead of the changeover, and that those who do not stay with either organization will receive severance.

Kootenai Health, a Northern Idaho nonprofit health system, is reportedly trimming 80 positions, or about 2% of its 4,500-plus workforce.

The system told Coeur d'Alene Press that it has been pressured by slow-to-increase Medicare reimbursement, higher expenses, commercial payment delays and the loss of statutory discounts when its primary 397-bed hospital no longer qualified as a 340B Disproportionate Share Hospital two years back. It also pointed to a rising population in its communities, driving a need for additional investments into more hospital space to meet demand.

The system did not outline what types of roles are affected, but said it still at the moment has 139 other positions that are open.

Healthcare generative AI company Abridge recently cut its workforce as part of an "organization-wide realignment," the company confirmed to Fierce Healthcare on Friday.

It has been revealed that the organization did not disclose how many staff were impacted by the layoffs. Abridge, founded in 2018, has raised more than $750 million in venture capital funding to date. The company works with more than 300 health systems and is projected to support more than 100 million clinical conversations this year.

"We’re in a rare moment in health care and AI, and we’re realigning from a position of strength to flatten our organization and build and deliver products faster. This realignment will enable us to continue to grow, hire in priority areas, and invest in new opportunities," the company noted in a statement provided to Fierce Healthcare.

Abridge said it was supporting staff impacted by the cuts with "meaningful transition packages and outplacement transition support.".

Sources indicate that "Abridge is growing rapidly, reflected in both revenue growth and customer demand, and our pace of product development has accelerated significantly. As an AI-native company, we are realigning teams across the organization to further increase our pace of innovation. Abridge remains very well capitalized, and continues to hold more than a majority of the capital it has raised to date," the company mentioned.

Healthcare startup Heidi reduced its headcount by 18%, the company's CEO and co-founderTom Kelly revealed in a LinkedIn post on Thursday.

The firm did not disclose how many employees were impacted or what roles were cut. Heidi has more than 600 employees, so the cuts impacted about 108 staff.

Industry observers note that the company, which first launched in Australia, initially started as an ambient AI medical scribe and then expanded into point-of-care clinical guidelines with Heidi Evidence and AI hardware (Remote) for clinical work as well as a voice-to-text feature, called Dictate. Heidi says it now supports around 2.8 million patient interactions each week in 110 languages from 190 countries.

It has been revealed that "In the last few weeks, we reflected carefully on how we're structured, and we weren't putting our investment into the right teams and markets to make the most of our continuing growth. It's painful, but it's what we need to do now to continue growing swiftly and deliver on our prepares for next year," Kelly wrote in his LinkedIn post.

The company is providing severance and benefits packages that vary by country but "exceed statutory requirements in every location," he wrote.

"Heidi is growing rapidly because clinicians around the world need and want our technology. We are investing in expanding our products, markets and team, and now support three million patient interactions every week. Our team has helped make that possible," Kelly wrote in a note to staff posted to the tech giant's website. "After reviewing our priorities in detail, we’ve made difficult choices about where to focus our team and investment to deliver the greatest impact for customers going forward. That means bringing more customer support into product, bringing R&D together in one roadmap and giving our fresh product businesses clearer ownership and dedicated teams.".

Also this week, Kelly unveiled that two of Heidi’s three co-founders, Waleed Mussa and Lu Yui. are preparing to leave the startup. "Waleed and Yu built Heidi with me, and it’s going to be really hard for all of us to continue without them. They’re leaving for different reasons, with their transitions happening over the coming weeks and months," Kelly wrote in a LinkedIn post.

Mussa is leaving to spend more time with his family, while Yui will transition into an advisory role focused on models and hardware through the end of March next year, Kelly wrote.

In September, Heidi landed $340 million to fuel its push beyond clinical documentation into AI-powered workflow automation and agentic capabilities for clinicians. The company raised $100 million series C funding. Alongside the equity round, Heidi also secured a $240 million growth investment led by General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund.

Children's Mercy, a pediatric health system based in Kansas City, Missouri, confirmed to press that it is cutting 115 positions, or about 1.2% of its total workforce.

The organization, in a statement, attributed the decision to "rising costs and reimbursement that has not kept pace." Among those affected, "most are non-clinical administrative, leadership and support roles," the statement reads.

Concurrent with the cuts was word that 473 of the system's revenue cycle and scheduling employees are shifting over to revenue cycle management vendor Ensemble, where they'll continue to work with Children's Mercy.

In April, the children's hospital unveiled aims to build a new acute patient tower at its flagship location in response to "increasing demand for highly specialized pediatric care as general hospitals nationwide reduce pediatric capacity." The project will expand total capacity by 25% to 30%, cost more than $1 billion and target a 2031 completion.

Rural Colorado nonprofit Montrose Regional Health, which includes a single 75-bed hospital and other clinical locations, announced this week a restructuring that eliminated 77 positions.

Of these, 43 were vacant and 34 were filled by current employees. Nearly half of the total positions were direct patient care roles, and 12 were leadership.

The system, in a release, said its volumes have grown about 10% over the past year while commercial reimbursement stayed flat and expenses rose. Its decision came after restricting hiring and capital spending, cost reduction efforts and other measures to reduce losses and limit outstanding insurance payments for care already delivered, and will save over $8 million annually.

The system stated it does not have other workforce reductions planned at this time. The changes are not expected to affect "critical hospital-based services," though some service lines will be changing as part of the restructuring.

Specialty cancer care provider City of Hope filed a Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification outlining aims to permanently lay off 73 employees, effective Nov. 24.

The organization, in a statement to Becker's, stated most of those affected work in business support and will receive support services like transition benefits and severance. The cuts will not directly affect patient care, they said.

Kaiser Permanente is laying off 147 workers across multiple Northern and Southern California locations, the country's largest nonprofit health system reported in Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification filings.

The reductions are effective on Nov. 20, and per the filing affect workers reporting to corporate and administrative offices.

The system, in statements to press, affirmed that the affected positions "do not provide direct patient care." The organization noted some workers are looking at other openings within the system, though severance, career support and outplacement services are also being extended to others "where appropriate.".

SAC Health, a San Bernadino nonprofit chain of clinics, laid off 52 more workers shortly after a prior round of 49 cuts.

According to recent reports, the changes were reported in a Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification filing and, in a prior internal memo and more recent statement to press, described the decision as necessary to strengthen operations. Both rounds of cuts involved nonclinical workers, with the former closely following the closure of two clinics.

The organization said that patient care and services are continuing through the latest cuts without interruption, and, in an internal memo provided to employees, that no additional reorganization is planned.

Catholic Health is eliminating 40 positions across five of its locations and realigning 34 other roles, according to a Sept. 22 press release shared with Fierce Healthcare.

It has been revealed that the layoffs affect both union and non-union positions at Catholic Health’s Administrative and Regional Training Center, Mercy Hospital of Buffalo, Mount St. Mary’s Hospital, Sisters of Charity Hospital and St. Joseph Campus.

The health system is working with affected employees to review potential placement opportunities in current openings, the announcement said.

Moreover, 34 positions within Mercy Hospital are being realigned as “volumes surge” in its emergency department. Impacted employees will be able to transition directly into current vacancies within the hospital.

According to recent reports, “These are difficult decisions because they affect valued members of our Catholic Health family who have contributed greatly to our organization and the communities we serve,” said Joyce Markiewicz, Catholic Health president and CEO, in a statement. “We are committed to treating every affected associate with dignity, compassion, and respect while ensuring Catholic Health remains strong and positioned to fulfill our mission well into the future.”.

It has been revealed that peaceHealth is planning to cut 150 positions across its facilities on Nov. 20, according to a notice filed with the Washington State Employment Security Department.

Bumping rights do not exist for any impacted positions, the Sept. 17 notice stated.

Fierce Healthcare has reached out to PeaceHealth for additional comment.

Elevance Health is laying off 216 positions in Louisiana as it prepares for its contract expiration with Medicaid in the state.

The organization disclosed the plans in a Sept. 15 notice (PDF), in which it remarked the cuts would be effective Dec. 31. Louisiana’s Medicaid contract with Healthy Blue is set to expire the same day.

“We are focused on supporting our associates through this transition with clear communication, career resources and redeployment opportunities across Elevance Health wherever possible,” the organization said in a statement to Fierce Healthcare. “We are grateful for their dedication to Louisiana Medicaid members since 2017.”.

Latest Hampshire's Dartmouth Health stated it notified 124 workers that their positions had been eliminated, while also shuttering 303 open roles at the Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center and Dartmouth Hitchcock Clinics Southern Region.

In a recent development, the adjustments, it mentioned, will see executive and administrative leadership roles consolidated and "select programs" eliminated or affected, including Tele-ICU and Tele-ED, the Upcoming England Alliance for Health and some in-house employee training programs. The system said it does not expect the changes to harm patients.

Recent findings suggest that “The employees affected by these changes have made meaningful contributions to Dartmouth Health, our patients and our communities,” Joanne M. Conroy, M.D., CEO and president of Dartmouth Health, said in a statement. “Some have spent many years serving this organization. The decision to eliminate a position or program does not diminish the value of the work these colleagues have done and the contributions they have made.”.

Those affected by the cuts will be "offered resources, transition support and opportunities to pursue other roles within the health system," the system noted.

Dartmouth Health noted that its operating expenses, particularly around labor, supply and drug costs, have outpaced patient revenues. Ahead of the cuts, it mentioned it has already worked to reduce some expenses by reducing travel and conference participation, reducing staffing reliance on traveler positions and strategic capital deployment to expand capacity and meet demand.

According to recent reports, A restructuring at University of Vermont Health will see 199 positions eliminated in late October, about 55 of which will be reconfigured into new positions, leadership unveiled in a Sept. 15 staff email and confirmed to press.

The changes are a second round of layoffs for the academic system, when another restructuring saw 142 roles condensed into 66. Leadership attributed both to state mandates to reduce spending and other financial pressures.

Some displaced medical staff will be able to apply for other roles at the system, Leffler remarked, and include leadership along with others. More than half of the affected roles are at the system's main medical center.

Recent findings suggest that "As we’ve discussed in our town hall meetings, our health system is facing a major budget shortfall, and we’re relying on our savings to pay the bills," system CEO and University of Vermont Medical Center President Stephen Leffler, M.D., wrote to staff. "That can’t continue.".

Some displaced medical staff will be able to apply for other roles at the system, Leffler mentioned, and include leadership along with others. More than half of the affected roles are at the system's main medical center.

Leffler also noted that the organization has cut 17% of its executive positions in the past year, axed "at-risk pay" for leaders and will be withholding raises for "most" senior leaders.

Conifer Health Solutions, the revenue cycle business of for-profit Tenet Healthcare, plans to permanently lay off 1,037 employees as a result of its breakup with CommonSpirit Health, according to a mandatory notice filing with the Texas Workforce Commission.

The layoffs are set to begin on Nov. 2, according to the WARN filing, and involve workers who report to Tenet’s corporate headquarters in Dallas. Affected workers are not represented by a union and do not have any bumping rights. Read the full story here.

Hundreds of workers at nonprofit health system Trinity Health's Livonia, Michigan headquarters will be permanently laid off, according to a WARN filing with the state.

Trinity had signaled the staffing change back in June when it declared some in-house technology and information services work would be transitioned to an unspecified technology partner organization. That prior statement and the WARN filing outline positions that do not directly face patients.

Recent findings suggest that "The pace and complexity of health care technology are accelerating," Trinity stated in June. "Sustaining that pace is increasingly difficult for any single organization on its own. A partner whose core business is technology support gives us access to specialized expertise and innovation at the speed and scale health care now requires while strengthening service reliability.​".

According to recent reports, the cuts are scheduled to begin Oct. 25 and run through Nov. 29. Trinity previously suggested that some of the affected workers would have "opportunities for new roles within Trinity Health and the partner organization along with transition support and resources.​".

For-profit hospital chain HCA Healthcare confirmed an unspecified number of layoffs in an emailed statement.

The system noted the cuts represented "a small percentage of positions across our corporate office and support functions." It said the changes are a response to pressures like rising costs, shifting policy and increasing numbers of uninsured patients (HCA recently lowered its 2026 earnings forecast on worse-than-anticipated quarterly results).

The organization noted it would be providing "a range of resources including severance and recruitment and outplacement support" to those affected, and noted that it is still hiring for other roles across its national footprint.

Academic health system Stanford Health Care has disclosed looks to trim 95 employees, or around 0.5% of its more than 18,000-person workforce.

The organization disclosed the looks in an Aug. 28 California WARN filing, in which it said the cuts would be effective Nov. 2.

In a statement given to Fierce Healthcare, Stanford described the cuts as part of a regular review of its operations and patient needs.

None of the affected positions provide direct patient care, it said, and are located in its Technology and Digital Solutions department (79 workers, according to the WARN filing) as well as other administrative areas (16 workers).

"We are providing active support for redeployment within the organization where possible and opening new roles with the opportunity for impacted employees to apply," the statement reads.

Sources indicate that walnut Creek, California-based John Muir Health reported prepares to lay off 78 workers, according to an Aug. 27 WARN filing .

Industry observers note that the cuts will be effective Oct. 28 and span multiple sections of the nonprofit system. According to the filing, affected roles work in finance, human resources, marketing, IT, management and clinical care.

John Muir Health, in a statement, mentioned that the layoffs impact about 1% of its workforce and "are mainly focused on leadership positions, employees in administrative services and employees who do not provide direct patient care.".

The system noted national and state policy headwinds like the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and California's 2030 seismic mandate, respectively, for its decision to proactively tighten its headcount.

Impacted employees have been notified, and any who do not find another position within the organization will receive a severance package offer, the statement reads.

Minnesota insurer UCare will layoff 102 employees as it continues to wind down its business.

Per a Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) posting on Aug. 3, the organization will no longer support some of its Medicaid plans, which were sold to Medica, as of Oct. 1. As such, the layoffs are permanent.

Impacted employees include individuals working at its headquarters as well as workers who are primarily or exclusively remote.

Effected employees will work their last day in October, with one staying on until November, according to the notice. They will continue to be paid through the notice window.

UCare revealed last November that it would begin to sunset its business operations following massive losses.

MaineHealth mentioned in a statement that it will be adjusting partis of its IT and analytics departments, leading to layoffs for 83 non-patient-facing employees.

Fifty-six of the cuts are among IT, while the remaining 27 in analytics stem from the consolidation of three separate teams into a single, 36-person unit. MaineHealth stated that current employees in both departments "will participate in a selection process for roles in the redesigned organizations," but that "unfortunately not every affected care team member will have a role in the future-state IT and Analytics departments.".

The system employs about 24,000 people, and stated it will be "actively seeking opportunities elsewhere within" the organization "whenever possible before any employment separation occurs.".

MaineHealth remarked the reorganization was prompted by changes in policy and reimbursement, as well as technology and patient demand.

Sources indicate that tower Health filed a Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification report with the state of Pennsylvania disclosing plans to lay off 160 at its Pottstown Hospital, effective Sept. 28.

The system, in a statement, noted that the "difficult workforce decisions" come amid a multi-million-dollar overhaul that will expand the hospital's ED, boost behavioral health services and "patch portions of the hospital while realigning certain services to better reflect current patient demand and the realities of today's healthcare environment.".

Industry observers note that the statement did not outline any potential separation benefits being provided to those affected. The cuts represent over a fifth of the hospital's total headcount.

Wellstar Health System laid off 761 workers yesterday “following a comprehensive review of our organization,” the Georgia nonprofit confirmed to Fierce Healthcare.

Sources indicate that the cuts translate to roughly 2% of the organization’s 35,000-plus workforce and excluded any frontline care roles, Wellstar said. Rather, the layoffs “impact our corporate and shared services functions, as well as certain administrative roles within Wellstar Medical Group,” it said in the statement. Read more.

Novant Health confirmed to press it would be eliminating 31 jobs across the organization as part of an effort "to modernize our revenue cycle operations.".

The cuts are intended to head off redundancy at the 44,000-person system, and part of a regular evaluation of organizational structure, it told press.

Recent findings suggest that "Decisions affecting team members are never made lightly," a spokesperson remarked. "While these changes are necessary to help ensure the long-term sustainability of our organization and our ability to serve patients, we recognize the impact on those affected and are committed to providing transition support. We are grateful for their contributions to Novant Health and our patients.".

Two Dignity Health hospitals, part of CommonSpirit Health, reported layoffs affecting 139 workers in recent WARN filings.

Fifty-seven of those cuts are at Bakersfield Memorial Hospital, in central California, with the remaining 82 at Los Angeles' California Hospital Medical Center.

In a recent development, A representative for CommonSpirit confirmed the layoffs and in a statement said the organization was "realigning our resources and enhancing operational efficiencies" for the long term. The statement did not address any potential separation benefits or services.

Recent findings suggest that "At Bakersfield Memorial Hospital and California Hospital Medical Center, we are committed to delivering exceptional care and being a strong, sustainable partner in the health of our communities," the statement read. "Maintaining this commitment is difficult given the financial landscape impacting healthcare systems across the country which have impacted our business as well.".

Roseville, California-based Adventist Health confirmed 132 layoffs stemming from the system's decision to centralize quality, risk management, infection prevention and accreditation functions that were previously handled at the hospital level.

Sources indicate that the cuts span several hospitals, according to a WARN filing. Of those affected, 109 have been offered latest roles at the system.

"To ensure we have strong accountability and deep expertise in these notable functions, we have worked thoughtfully to create alignment of positions and centralization of roles. This new structure will advance our mission of compassionate, whole-person care—connecting dedicated local team members with best practices from system-level experts.".

Industry observers note that central Oregon's St. Charles Health System has overhauled its leadership structure, announcing the elimination of 22 filled and 23 open supervisor and above roles "in support services areas of the organization.".

The cuts do not impact any direct patient care positions, and are hitting less than 1% of the four-hospital nonprofit's total workforce. It said the decision was made in response to the rapid growth in scale and demand its seen in recent years, and a need to adjust its structure for continuing increases.

Recent findings suggest that “The changes we are making today are about setting ourselves up for a more sustainable and scalable structure for the future and I want to reassure our community that St. Charles is strong, stable and committed to meeting community needs,” Michael Hartke, incoming president and CEO, mentioned in the announcement.

University of Missouri Health Care (MU Health Care) shared news of an "organizational redesign" that includes a 74-employee workforce reduction.

The cuts largely landed in non-clinical and administrative areas, with the system noting that "in some areas, staffing levels exceeded those of comparable organizations, while in others, operational assessments identified opportunities to add positions and better align resources with patient and operational needs.".

Those affected were offered transition resources, such as benefits continuation and other internal job opportunities, with the notice highlighting more than 500 other positions that are currently open across the system.

Industry observers note that "Healthcare is changing rapidly, and our organization must evolve with it," Ric Ransom, CEO, remarked in the announcement. "These decisions are difficult, but they are necessary to ensure MU Health Care remains strong, competitive and capable of serving patients and communities for generations to come.".

It has been revealed that other changes at the system include tweaks to various employee benefit programs that would require board approval "including retirement contributions," and the closure of four retail health clinics. At the same time, it noted a plan to boost other benefits like dependent care assistance and expansions of some urgent care and imaging services.

"These actions are not simply about reducing costs," remarked Ransom. "They are about aligning our organization with the realities of modern health care, improving how we serve patients and ensuring we can continue investing in our people, our mission and the communities that rely on us.".

Lovelace Health System has laid off "approximately 43 positions," or about 1.6% of its local workforce, a representative told Fierce Healthcare in a statement.

Industry observers note that the cuts are primarily in administrative and support positions, and the system looked to curb the impact by placing some of its employees in other open roles, the representative said. The system is "supporting affected team members through this transition," but did not specify whether that includes severance or other benefits.

In a recent development, "These are difficult decisions, and we don't take them lightly," the statement reads. "Like health systems across the country, we are facing rising costs, shifting payor dynamics and a challenging policy environment. These actions reflect deliberate steps to manage costs and ensure our structure keeps pace with current realities.".

Lovelace is a five-hospital system based in Albuquerque, New Mexico, and is owned and operated by publicly traded for-profit Ardent Healthcare.

BSA Health System, a three-hospital system serving Texas' Panhandle region, is cutting 29 of its staff, or 1% of its local workforce, according to a local media report.

The system is part of Ardent Healthcare, and appears to be providing press with a near-identical statement on the decision as Lovelace Health System (above) pointing to "rising costs, shifting payor dynamics and a challenging policy environment." Fierce Healthcare has reached out to BSA Health System for confirmation.

UPMC, the nonprofit system that stands as Pennsylvania's largest non-governmental employer, confirmed it is cutting about 200 employees and shuttering 300 open positions that were not in active recruitment.

A spokesperson organization, which employs about 100,000 total and operates more than 40 hospitals, mentioned the reductions are "primarily among those who are not in clinical or member-facing roles." The system will also be giving "enhanced severance pay and benefits coverage for affected employees," they said.

Industry observers note that UPMC recorded $33.6 billion in total operating revenue across 2025 as well as a 0.9% operating margin. The layoffs come about two years after the organization conducting a more sweeping reduction of 1,100 workers two years ago, noted one of the nurse unions active in UPMC's hospitals.

"In that previous round of cuts, we lost many experienced and valued clinicians with roles in direct patient care and nurse education," Michelle Hart, a neonatal nurse practitioner and member of Magee Nurses and Advanced Practitioners United, SEIU Healthcare PA, said in a statement. "When UPMC reduces staff, those duties often then fall on nurses when we already do not have enough time with our patients to provide the level of care we believe in. ... UPMC cannot continue to prioritize branding, construction and executive compensation over investing in frontline staff.".

University of Vermont Health said this week it has eliminated 142 positions in Vermont and Northern Latest York, of which 76 are permanent deletions and 66 will be reposted with adjusted job descriptions.

The academic system noted most of the changes weren't in areas providing direct patient care, but that some comprised "targeted clinical changes where necessary." It added that more employees were informed that their positions or departments are in the midst of reorganization.

The organization attributed its decisions to "significant financial shortfalls.".

Recent findings suggest that “These are extremely difficult decisions because of their impact on our valued colleagues,” UVM Health CEO Stephen Leffler, M.D., stated in a release on the cuts. “We must make these hard choices to ensure we can continue to provide high-quality care that is accessible and more affordable for the communities we serve.”.

UVM Health said it's working with employees' unions through the layoffs, and that those affected are being offered transition support and a chance to apply to other roles. Its cuts follow smaller cuts at its Northern New York earlier this year that affected nine workers, and a more substantial round last July that hit 146 positions.

Centra Health, a nonprofit system serving central and southern Virginia, shared news of a restructuring that will lead to "approximately 90" layoffs, or about 1% of its total workforce.

It has been revealed that of those affected, the system said 35 are being offered other open positions for which they are qualified. Eligible employees will receive severance as well as continued healthcare coverage under COBRA. Centra added that it has "used natural attrition" over the past several months, deciding not to refill positions as former employees left.

Centra mentioned the restructure is part of a broader initiative focused on spotting redundancies and efficiencies, "particularly in administrative functions," and will help "adapt to the significant pressures facing healthcare providers including reductions in government reimbursements, economic challenges, shifting demographics and evolving technologies.".

Baptist Health has shared word that it is eliminating around 70 workers in Arkansas' Fort Smith area.

A statement on the decision shared with press pointed to "a sustained decrease in service volumes and the duplication of certain roles." The system added that the cuts will not affect care services, and that those impacted will receive severance and job placement services.

Of note, the news comes less than two months after Baptist announced aims to ax 150 other employees in the same area as a result of service line changes.

Optum will layoff 58 workers across three divisions based in the Garden State, according to Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act notices.

It has been revealed that the largest share of those layoffs are at Optum Services, where 36 positions will be eliminated. Five jobs will be cut at Optum Care, and 17 people will be laid off at Optum Select Management. The layoffs are effective on Aug. 26, according to the document.

Optum had not yet returned a request for comment at the time of publication.

Washington Regional Medical System, northwest Arkansas' largest healthcare provider, announced a "strategic organizational restructuring" it stated will reduce its workforce by 86 people.

The nonprofit said it will be consolidating certain management and support functions, while also redesigning its workflows to reduce administrative burdens. The decision is a response to financial pressures including heightened labor and supply costs as well as "continued reimbursement challenges.".

“We are all evaluating our business and implementing significant operational changes,” Washington Regional President and CEO Lucas Campbell, M.D., in the announcement. “By restructuring our management operations and consolidating roles, Washington Regional will reduce redundancies and optimize efficiency while still providing the high-quality care our community has come to expect.”.

In a recent development, the system said there will be no disruptions in patient care due to the changes. It did not specify whether benefits, severance or other support is being provided to affected employees.

Care Latest England noted it has laid off more than 30 nonclinical and leadership jobs "as part of a restructuring in response to ongoing financial pressures that continue to strain hospitals and healthcare providers throughout Rhode Island.".

Employees affected by the restructuring will received unspecified "resources and assistance" from the system, according to the announcement.

Care Latest England mentioned it has been working to address an estimated $20 million budget shortfall for the 2026 fiscal year. Its announcement of the cuts pointed to low Medicaid reimbursement rates, rising expenses and greater demand for uncompensated care, and included calls for state leaders to back a proposed funding package.

In a recent development, “Without meaningful action, Rhode Island risks continued erosion of healthcare access, longer emergency room wait times, reduced services, and additional job losses throughout the healthcare sector," President and CEO Michael Wagner, M.D., said. "We urge state leaders to prioritize investments that strengthen healthcare and protect access to care for all Rhode Islanders.”.

Closures and consolidations across 10 Intermountain Health clinics in Montana and Colorado will hit 93 of the nonprofit system's employees, according to statements given to press.

Sources indicate that in Montana, the system prepares to close a family medicine clinic and "shift the model of care" at four of its other clinics. In Colorado, Intermountain plans to close two occupational health clinics and a sports medicine clinic, while also planning to fold an endocrinology clinic into a primary care clinic and shuttering some services at an obesity management clinic.

It has been revealed that forty-one of the cuts are among "leader and staff member roles" in Montana, with Colorado employees comprising the remainder. The changes are scheduled to take effect from early June through late July, depending on the site.

Intermountain's statement chalked the decisions up to strengthening "long-term financial sustainability in an increasingly volatile healthcare industry." It said employees whose roles are impacted may apply for other open positions, and that they will be given access to "transition support, career assistance, severance (where applicable) and benefits guidance.".

It has been revealed that health tech manufacturer Innovaccer reduced its workforce, primarily impacting positions outside the United States, the company confirmed to Fierce Healthcare. Inc42 reported that the company laid off 340 employees, impacting staff in India and the U.S.

In a statement, Innovaccer stated the workforce reduction was related to its shift to AI-enabled operations.

"As an AI-native health technology manufacturer, Innovaccer is applying its own automation principles internally. We are building an organization that is lean, fast and focused, which prioritizes speed and measurable outcomes for our customers," the company mentioned.

It's the manufacturer's third layoff round in the past four years, Inc42 reported.

The company, founded in 2014, built software solutions that aggregate patient data across care settings and systems. Innovaccer secured a $275 million series F funding round in January 2025 to invest in artificial intelligence with the goal of becoming a “one-stop shop” for healthcare AI solutions.

The firm has raised $675 million to date with a post-money valuation of approximately $3.45 billion following its series F round.

Forty jobs are in the firing line of a rehashed behavioral health model at Providence Sacred Heart Medical Center.

Other mental health support roles in the ED and adult geriatric psych unit will also change over to a new staffing model that relies on certified nursing assistants with specialized behavioral health training, it said.

There will be no interruption in behavioral service availability during the shift, Providence remarked.

The nation's largest for-profit health system confirmed Monday an undisclosed number of non-clinical layoffs.

Service line changes at Baptist Health will hit 150 employees' roles over the next 60 days.

The cuts are tied to the system's Baptist Health Fort Smith hospital, which the tech giant noted has lost a cumulative $127 million from 2018 through March 2026. To avoid closure, services including obstetrics, oncology, nephrology, pulmonary and infectious disease care have or will soon wind down, with other affiliated clinics also set to shutter.

"By stabilizing our foundation now, we stop the cycle of unsustainable losses and create a platform from which we can eventually grow and even add services back," the organization wrote in a statement for press.

Oregon Health & Science University noted it is cutting 59 positions tied to its Knight Cancer Institute.

Nine employees at two University of Vermont Health hospitals in northern Fresh York were reportedly eliminated in response to cost and policy pressures.

UnityPoint Health, which employs 31,000 people, said this week it will be eliminating 207 of its IT roles amid a transition of their responsibilities to third-party vendors.

Additional cuts are on the way for the system's revenue cycle workers, though how many will be affected has not yet been determined.

Those being laid off are being provided with severance, benefits continuation and other career transition support.

Baylor Scott & White Health Plan, the insurance arm of the nonprofit Texas system, shared looks exit the individual marketplaces as well as Medicaid, a move it mentioned will impact 321 jobs.

Advanced Specialty Hospitals of Toledo's May 1 closure will see 116 workers permanently laid off, effective June 8, according to a Workers Adjustment and Retraining Notification filing.
